one_line: For mature organ benchmarks, the residual model-vs-reference gap is annotation protocol disagreement, not model error.
problem: Benchmarks report residual Dice gaps that drive method development, but it is unknown how much of that gap is achievable at all given rater disagreement.
core_hypothesis: On well-benchmarked large organs, top models already sit inside the inter-rater disagreement band; the residual gap measures protocol ambiguity rather than model deficiency.
falsifiable_prediction: With fresh multi-rater re-annotation of an existing organ test set, model-vs-rater disagreement will be statistically indistinguishable from rater-vs-rater disagreement for a majority of large organs.
why_important: If true, continued leaderboard chasing on these organs is measurement noise, and effort should shift to protocol standardization and genuinely unsolved structures.
why_possibly_novel: Inter-rater variability is often reported descriptively, but the specific null hypothesis that a trained model is an exchangeable rater on existing benchmarks is rarely tested formally.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select one public abdominal CT organ test set; obtain three independent expert re-annotations of about 30 cases; run equivalence tests comparing model-rater versus rater-rater Dice and surface distance distributions.
main_risk: Expert re-annotation is costly, and ambiguity may be organ-specific, weakening any general claim.
community_default_belief: Residual benchmark gaps reflect model limitations that better architectures or training will close.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Reference masks are single-rater products of ambiguous protocols, so the target itself carries irreducible variance that bounds achievable scores.
fastest_falsification: If model-rater disagreement significantly exceeds rater-rater disagreement on most re-annotated organs, the hypothesis is false.

one_line: Boundary label noise in 3D medical data is anisotropic and systematic because annotators trace in-plane, and models inherit a slice-direction-dependent boundary bias.
problem: Label noise in volumetric segmentation is usually modeled as isotropic random perturbation, ignoring how annotation is physically performed slice by slice.
core_hypothesis: Out-of-plane (through-slice) boundary labels are systematically biased and noisier than in-plane boundaries, and trained models reproduce this anisotropic error pattern.
falsifiable_prediction: Surface error of both labels and model predictions, decomposed by surface-normal direction, will be significantly larger for surfaces normal to the acquisition axis, and retraining on reoriented volumes will rotate the error pattern accordingly.
why_important: Anisotropic label bias corrupts volumetry and margin decisions in a directionally structured way that isotropic noise-robust methods cannot fix.
why_possibly_novel: Noise-robust segmentation work typically assumes direction-independent noise; a directional decomposition of label error tied to annotation mechanics is rarely the object of study.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a dataset with near-isotropic voxels, compare per-surface-normal boundary disagreement between two rater sets; train identical models on axial versus reformatted coronal annotations and test whether error anisotropy follows the annotation plane.
main_risk: Anisotropic acquisition resolution confounds annotation-plane effects; needs isotropic data to separate the two.
community_default_belief: Label noise is approximately random and can be averaged out with enough data or noise-robust losses.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Annotation is a physical in-plane act; its errors are structured by the viewing plane and are learned as systematic bias, not variance.
fastest_falsification: If boundary error shows no dependence on surface orientation relative to the annotation plane on isotropic data, the hypothesis fails.

one_line: Annotator identity is decodable from masks alone, and annotator-style normalization improves cross-dataset transfer more than image harmonization.
problem: Cross-dataset segmentation transfer is treated as an image-domain problem, while systematic differences in who drew the labels are ignored.
core_hypothesis: Each annotator or annotating institution has a stable, learnable contouring style (margin tightness, smoothing, inclusion rules), and this style is a first-order component of cross-dataset performance gaps.
falsifiable_prediction: A classifier will predict annotator or source institution from mask geometry alone well above chance, and style-conditioning or style-normalizing labels will recover a substantial share of the cross-dataset Dice drop without touching the images.
why_important: If label style, not image appearance, drives much of the domain gap, the field is optimizing the wrong pipeline stage with image harmonization and domain adaptation.
why_possibly_novel: Rater bias is known in quality-assurance literature, but treating contouring style as a transferable, conditionable variable inside segmentation training is not standard practice.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On any dataset with per-rater metadata, train a mask-only rater classifier; then train a segmentation model with a rater-conditioning token and test cross-rater generalization against an unconditioned baseline.
main_risk: Public datasets rarely release annotator identity, limiting where the hypothesis can be tested.
community_default_belief: Cross-dataset gaps are caused mainly by scanner and population shift in the images.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The supervision target changes across datasets too; models fit the labeling function, and different institutions implement different labeling functions.
fastest_falsification: If mask-only classifiers cannot beat chance at identifying the annotating source, style is not a stable learnable signal and the hypothesis collapses.

one_line: Many 3D reference masks are sparse-slice annotations completed by interpolation, and models trained on them learn interpolation artifacts as anatomy.
problem: Dataset construction details such as slice-skipping plus interpolation are undocumented, yet they define the geometry statistics of the ground truth.
core_hypothesis: Models trained on interpolation-completed labels acquire an over-smooth surface prior whose curvature statistics match the interpolation operator rather than true anatomy.
falsifiable_prediction: Surface curvature spectra of model predictions will match interpolated-label statistics and differ measurably from densely annotated reference surfaces of the same organs; training on densely annotated subsets will shift predictions toward higher-frequency surfaces.
why_important: Smoothness that comes from annotation shortcuts silently erases fine anatomical detail relevant for surgical planning and early pathology.
why_possibly_novel: The interpolation step of dataset creation is almost never treated as a bias source with measurable spectral signatures in model outputs.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Densely annotate a small set of organs at every slice; compare curvature and surface-frequency statistics between dense labels, interpolated labels, and predictions of models trained on each.
main_risk: True anatomy may genuinely be smooth for many organs, making the effect small except for detailed structures.
community_default_belief: Reference masks represent expert-perceived anatomy at the dataset resolution.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Annotation economics force sparse tracing; the completion operator, not the expert, decides fine-scale geometry.
fastest_falsification: If model surface statistics are indistinguishable between dense-trained and interpolated-trained versions, the artifact-learning claim fails.

one_line: Label errors concentrate at pathology and low-contrast interfaces, so uniform-noise-robust training fails precisely where errors are clinically costly.
problem: Noise-robust segmentation methods are validated with synthetic uniform or random-boundary noise, but real annotation errors are input-dependent.
core_hypothesis: Real label error rate is a strong function of local image evidence (contrast, pathology presence), and methods tuned on uniform synthetic noise select for exactly the wrong robustness mechanism.
falsifiable_prediction: A map of rater disagreement will correlate strongly with local contrast and pathology masks; noise-robust methods that win under synthetic uniform noise will show no advantage, or a disadvantage, under real multi-rater noise in low-contrast regions.
why_important: Method rankings from synthetic-noise benchmarks may be anti-predictive for clinical robustness where errors matter most.
why_possibly_novel: The mismatch between synthetic noise models and spatially structured, evidence-dependent real annotation noise is rarely quantified head-to-head for segmentation.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Use any multi-rater dataset to build an empirical noise model conditioned on local contrast; re-evaluate two or three published noise-robust training schemes under empirical versus uniform noise and compare rank stability.
main_risk: Empirical noise models require multi-rater data, and conclusions may not transfer across modalities.
community_default_belief: Robustness to injected random label noise implies robustness to real annotation noise.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Real noise is correlated with image difficulty, so it shifts decision boundaries systematically instead of adding variance the model can average out.
fastest_falsification: If rater disagreement shows no meaningful correlation with local contrast or pathology, the structured-noise premise is wrong.

one_line: Test labels in merged medical benchmarks are noisier than train labels, so the evaluation noise floor, not modeling, dominates leaderboard deltas.
problem: Merged and re-distributed benchmark test sets accumulate conversion, resampling, and curation errors whose magnitude relative to reported method differences is unknown.
core_hypothesis: On several popular segmentation benchmarks, the test-set label error alone induces score variability comparable to or larger than typical claimed method improvements.
falsifiable_prediction: Independent expert audit of a random test subset will find label defects whose correction changes per-method scores by amounts comparable to published between-method gaps, and re-ranking after correction will not preserve leaderboard order.
why_important: If leaderboard gaps sit inside the label-error band, published progress on these benchmarks is partly unfalsifiable.
why_possibly_novel: Label audits exist for classification test sets; systematic audits of segmentation test masks with re-ranking analysis are far less common.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sample 50 test cases from one widely used benchmark; have two experts flag and correct defects; recompute scores of several publicly available models before and after correction and test ranking stability.
main_risk: Audit itself introduces a new rater bias; needs adjudication protocol.
community_default_belief: Test annotations are trustworthy enough that score differences of one or two Dice points reflect real method differences.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Test sets are curated once, rarely re-audited, and inherit errors from format conversions and single-rater annotation under time pressure.
fastest_falsification: If audited corrections change model scores by an order of magnitude less than method gaps, the noise-floor claim fails.

one_line: Training on raw per-rater masks as separate supervision samples yields calibrated boundary uncertainty for free, beating post-hoc uncertainty methods.
problem: Multi-rater annotations are usually fused into a single consensus mask before training, discarding the disagreement structure that clinical users actually need.
core_hypothesis: A vanilla segmentation network trained on unfused per-rater masks converges to the empirical rater distribution at boundaries, providing spatial uncertainty that matches held-out rater disagreement better than ensembles or MC-dropout applied to consensus-trained models.
falsifiable_prediction: On held-out multi-rater cases, softmax probabilities of the rater-sampled model will match empirical rater agreement fractions more closely (lower calibration error against rater distribution) than ensemble or dropout uncertainty from consensus training.
why_important: It would provide clinically meaningful ambiguity maps without any specialized probabilistic machinery, changing default practice for multi-rater data.
why_possibly_novel: Probabilistic segmentation research focuses on dedicated generative or ensemble architectures; the simple baseline of not fusing raters is rarely evaluated as the primary uncertainty method against them.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On one multi-rater dataset, train the same architecture on consensus masks versus rater-sampled masks; compare voxelwise predicted probability to held-out rater agreement fractions.
main_risk: With few raters per case the empirical distribution is coarse and the learned probabilities may be poorly resolved.
community_default_belief: Consensus fusion improves label quality, and uncertainty should be added by dedicated probabilistic methods afterwards.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Fusion destroys exactly the signal uncertainty methods try to reconstruct; keeping raters separate preserves it in the loss directly.
fastest_falsification: If the rater-sampled model's probabilities fit held-out rater disagreement no better than consensus-trained ensembles, the free-calibration claim is false.

one_line: Annotation guidelines drift during a labeling campaign, so early versus late cases in one dataset differ systematically and are temporally decodable.
problem: Datasets are treated as internally homogeneous, but labeling campaigns run for months while conventions are being clarified.
core_hypothesis: Within a single dataset, annotation date (or case index as its proxy) predicts systematic mask differences, and models fit an average of shifting conventions rather than a single labeling function.
falsifiable_prediction: A classifier will distinguish early-campaign from late-campaign masks above chance from mask geometry; splitting train and test by campaign time will show a within-dataset generalization gap absent in random splits.
why_important: Within-dataset protocol drift inflates apparent model error and contaminates any analysis that assumes exchangeable labels.
why_possibly_novel: Temporal ordering of annotation is essentially never analyzed as a variance component in segmentation datasets.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Obtain any dataset with annotation timestamps or sequential case ids; test mask-feature drift over time and compare temporal-split versus random-split evaluation of a fixed model.
main_risk: Timestamps are rarely published; case ordering may correlate with clinical case-mix changes rather than protocol drift.
community_default_belief: A curated dataset represents one consistent labeling protocol.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Protocols are living documents; ambiguity resolutions accumulate during a campaign and change what annotators draw.
fastest_falsification: If no temporal signal in mask statistics exists after controlling for case-mix, the drift hypothesis fails for that dataset.

one_line: Much boundary disagreement is ontological, not perceptual: raters disagree about anatomical definitions, and per-region definition-ambiguity maps predict where all models plateau.
problem: Rater disagreement is treated as perceptual noise, conflating cannot-see disagreement with cannot-agree-on-definition disagreement.
core_hypothesis: For structures with fuzzy anatomical definitions (organ boundaries at hila, vessel entry zones, gland tails), disagreement persists at high image quality, and these definitional zones form a fixed spatial map where every model's error saturates.
falsifiable_prediction: Rater disagreement in definitional zones will be nearly independent of image SNR and contrast, unlike perceptual zones; error maps of diverse architectures will share the same definitional hotspots.
why_important: It separates problems solvable by better models from problems solvable only by better ontology, redirecting research and benchmark design.
why_possibly_novel: Decomposing inter-rater variance into perceptual versus definitional components with an image-quality intervention is an uncommon experimental design in segmentation.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Have raters annotate the same anatomy at two image quality levels (native and degraded); regions where disagreement does not decrease with quality are definitional; test whether model errors of several architectures concentrate there.
main_risk: Image quality manipulation may alter rater behavior beyond perception, contaminating the decomposition.
community_default_belief: Better image quality and better models jointly reduce boundary disagreement everywhere.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Where the definition itself is contested, no amount of signal or capacity produces agreement.
fastest_falsification: If disagreement decreases uniformly with image quality across all regions, the definitional-zone concept is unnecessary.

one_line: Annotators systematically under-include ambiguous voxels, so trained models inherit an undersegmentation bias fixable by a global bias correction rather than new architectures.
problem: Segmentation error is treated as unbiased, but annotation psychology suggests asymmetric behavior: omission of uncertain voxels is cheaper for a rater than commission.
core_hypothesis: Reference masks are biased small relative to consensus-of-many, models replicate this bias, and a single learned isotropic boundary offset per structure removes most volumetric error for volumetry applications.
falsifiable_prediction: Against dense multi-rater consensus, both single-rater labels and model outputs will show statistically significant negative volume bias, and a per-structure morphological correction estimated on few cases will remove most of the volumetric error on held-out cases.
why_important: Volumetry drives therapy decisions; a two-line bias correction outperforming years of architecture work would reset priorities.
why_possibly_novel: Systematic direction of annotation bias, as opposed to its magnitude, is rarely measured or exploited as a correction target.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a multi-rater dataset, compute signed volume error of single raters and of a standard model against high-rater-count consensus; fit and test a per-structure offset correction.
main_risk: Bias direction may differ by structure and modality, making corrections non-universal.
community_default_belief: Segmentation errors are approximately symmetric around the true boundary and must be reduced by better models.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Rater incentives are asymmetric, and consensus-of-many reveals a consistent inclusion deficit that supervised models faithfully copy.
fastest_falsification: If signed volume errors of raters and models are centered on zero against dense consensus, there is no exploitable bias.

one_line: Quality-control passes smooth reference contours, deleting real high-frequency anatomy, so models are penalized for correctly predicting fine detail.
problem: Dataset QC is assumed to only remove errors, but QC reviewers often regularize contours toward smooth, canonical shapes.
core_hypothesis: Post-QC masks have systematically lower surface frequency content than pre-QC raw annotations, and evaluation against post-QC masks ranks detail-preserving models below over-smoothing models.
falsifiable_prediction: Where pre- and post-QC annotation versions exist, spectral analysis will show high-frequency attenuation after QC, and model rankings by boundary metrics will differ between the two reference versions, favoring smoother models post-QC.
why_important: If QC injects a smoothness prior into ground truth, benchmarks structurally discourage models that recover clinically relevant fine structure such as spiculations.
why_possibly_novel: QC is audited for error removal, virtually never for the statistical fingerprint it imposes on the label distribution.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Obtain or recreate a small annotation set with archived pre-QC versions; compare surface spectra and re-rank two models (one detail-preserving, one smooth) under each reference.
main_risk: Pre-QC annotations are rarely archived, and recreating QC realistically is hard.
community_default_belief: QC strictly improves label quality, so evaluating against QC-ed labels is strictly fairer.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Reviewers use smoothness as a proxy for correctness, which is invalid exactly for irregular pathology and detailed anatomy.
fastest_falsification: If QC leaves surface frequency statistics unchanged, the smoothing-injection claim fails immediately.

one_line: Networks fit boundary label noise late in training and interior evidence early, so per-structure early stopping at different epochs beats a single global stopping point.
problem: Memorization dynamics are well studied for classification label noise, but the spatial version for segmentation, where noise lives at boundaries, is unclear.
core_hypothesis: Learning is spatially staged: interior voxels are fit early and generalize, boundary-noise voxels are memorized late; the optimal stopping epoch therefore differs per structure according to its boundary ambiguity.
falsifiable_prediction: Tracking per-voxel agreement with a held-out second rater across epochs will show boundary agreement peaking earlier than final-epoch training accuracy; per-structure stopping epochs chosen on rater-agreement curves will outperform global early stopping on multi-rater test data.
why_important: It offers a training-schedule-level tool against label noise that requires no new losses or architectures.
why_possibly_novel: Memorization-timing analyses are rarely done voxelwise and per-structure in segmentation, and stopping is universally global.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On one multi-rater dataset, log per-epoch checkpoints, evaluate boundary-band versus interior agreement with held-out raters across epochs, and compare global versus per-structure stopping.
main_risk: Per-structure stopping requires either multiple heads or checkpoint ensembling, adding inference complexity.
community_default_belief: One validation-loss-based early stopping point is adequate for the whole multi-structure model.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Different structures have different noise levels, so their memorization onsets differ and a single epoch cannot be optimal for all.
fastest_falsification: If boundary agreement with held-out raters increases monotonically to the end of training for all structures, staged memorization is absent.

one_line: Dice is size-confounded: cross-method rankings flip when stratified by structure volume, and most claimed gains are small-structure operating-point changes.
problem: Mean Dice aggregates over structures whose sizes span orders of magnitude, hiding what a method actually changed.
core_hypothesis: A large fraction of reported improvements reduce to shifting the sensitivity-precision operating point on small structures, which stratified analysis and a matched-threshold comparison would reveal as non-improvements in shape recovery.
falsifiable_prediction: Re-evaluating public method pairs with volume-stratified Dice and with per-structure threshold matching will erase or invert a substantial share of published gaps.
why_important: It would show that leaderboard progress partially reflects re-tuned trade-offs rather than better boundary inference, changing how papers should report results.
why_possibly_novel: Size-stratified re-analysis with explicit operating-point matching is rarely applied retroactively to segmentation method comparisons.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take several publicly released model checkpoints on one multi-organ benchmark; recompute size-stratified metrics and matched-sensitivity comparisons; count how many pairwise conclusions survive.
main_risk: Public checkpoints for matched comparisons may be scarce; retraining introduces its own variance.
community_default_belief: Higher mean Dice means better segmentation ability across the board.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Mean Dice rewards recall on small structures disproportionately, so an operating-point shift masquerades as capability.
fastest_falsification: If stratified and matched re-analysis preserves nearly all pairwise rankings, the confounding claim is overstated.

one_line: Hausdorff-type metrics are so unstable under tiny mask perturbations that their own test-retest variance exceeds typical reported method deltas.
problem: Boundary metrics like HD95 are reported to two decimals, but their sensitivity to single-voxel outliers, resampling, and connected-component handling is rarely quantified.
core_hypothesis: For typical medical structures, metric-level noise (perturbing masks within label-noise magnitude, or re-running inference with benign nondeterminism) induces HD95 variation comparable to between-method differences claimed in the literature.
falsifiable_prediction: Repeated evaluation of one fixed model under voxel-level benign perturbations and stochastic inference will produce HD95 spreads overlapping the gaps between adjacent leaderboard entries.
why_important: If the measurement instrument is noisier than the effect sizes, boundary-metric-based conclusions need confidence intervals or should be replaced.
why_possibly_novel: Metric reliability studies exist, but a direct comparison of metric test-retest noise against the distribution of published effect sizes is uncommon.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take one trained model and one test set; generate 20 evaluation replicates via seed changes and one-voxel boundary perturbations within rater-noise bounds; compare replicate spread to published deltas on the same benchmark.
main_risk: Choice of perturbation model is contestable; too aggressive perturbations trivially inflate spread.
community_default_belief: Boundary metrics are more clinically meaningful and equally reliable compared to overlap metrics.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Max-type statistics are dominated by single outlier points and inherit instability that overlap metrics average away.
fastest_falsification: If replicate HD95 spread is an order of magnitude below published gaps, the instability claim fails.

one_line: For radiotherapy organs-at-risk, dose-based evaluation reorders segmentation models relative to Dice, so geometric metrics are not valid surrogates for treatment impact.
problem: Segmentation for radiotherapy is validated geometrically, while the clinical quantity of interest is dosimetric change, and the mapping between them is nonlinear and position-dependent.
core_hypothesis: Rank correlation between Dice-based and dose-metric-based model orderings is weak for organs near steep dose gradients, meaning model selection by Dice regularly picks dosimetrically inferior models.
falsifiable_prediction: Recomputing plans on contours from multiple models will show model rankings by dose-volume endpoints that disagree with Dice rankings for a nontrivial fraction of organ-plan combinations, concentrated near high-gradient regions.
why_important: It directly challenges the validation standard used to clear auto-contouring tools for clinical radiotherapy use.
why_possibly_novel: Dosimetric evaluation exists in medical physics, but systematic surrogacy analysis (how often geometric selection picks the dosimetrically wrong model) is rarely quantified across models.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Use an open treatment-planning system on a small cohort; generate contours from three models; run automated re-planning; compute rank agreement between geometric and dosimetric orderings per organ.
main_risk: Automated re-planning pipelines are laborious and plan optimizer settings add variance.
community_default_belief: Sufficiently high Dice and surface distance imply clinical acceptability for radiotherapy contours.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Dose impact depends on where errors sit relative to beams and gradients, which geometric metrics ignore entirely.
fastest_falsification: If dose-based and Dice-based rankings agree almost everywhere, surrogacy is adequate and the concern is minor.

one_line: Mean-over-cases Dice hides bimodal failure: catastrophic-failure rate is the clinically relevant statistic and is nearly uncorrelated with mean Dice among top methods.
problem: Aggregate reporting assumes unimodal error distributions, but deployment risk is driven by the tail of complete failures.
core_hypothesis: Among methods within a few Dice points of each other, per-case failure-rate (fraction of cases below a usability threshold) varies severalfold and is statistically independent of the mean, so mean-based selection does not select the safest model.
falsifiable_prediction: Across public checkpoints on one benchmark, the correlation between mean Dice and below-threshold failure rate within the top cluster of methods will be weak, and the mean-best model will not be the failure-rate-best model in most comparisons.
why_important: Clinical adoption decisions should hinge on tail behavior; current benchmarking practice cannot see it.
why_possibly_novel: Failure-rate reporting exists sporadically, but the decoupling claim among near-tied methods, which is what leaderboards decide between, is untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate five to ten public models per benchmark case; compute mean Dice and failure rates at several thresholds; test rank agreement within the top group.
main_risk: Threshold choice for failure is arbitrary and organ-dependent; needs sensitivity analysis.
community_default_belief: The model with the best average performance is the best candidate for deployment.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Averages are insensitive to rare catastrophic outputs, which dominate clinical risk and vary independently across training runs.
fastest_falsification: If failure-rate and mean-Dice rankings coincide across benchmarks, mean-based selection is safe and the critique is moot.

one_line: Conventions for scoring empty or absent structures silently decide benchmark winners, and recomputing leaderboards under alternative conventions reorders the top entries.
problem: When a structure is absent in ground truth or prediction, Dice is undefined and each benchmark picks an ad hoc convention (score one, score zero, exclude), which interacts with disease prevalence.
core_hypothesis: For benchmarks containing absent-structure cases, the choice among standard empty-case conventions changes aggregate scores enough to permute top-five rankings, meaning some published orderings are artifacts of a bookkeeping decision.
falsifiable_prediction: Recomputing published evaluation outputs under three empty-case conventions will change at least some adjacent pairwise orderings on benchmarks with nontrivial absence rates.
why_important: A hidden convention should not decide method rankings; the field needs explicit, prevalence-robust reporting.
why_possibly_novel: The empty-case issue is known to evaluation specialists but its actual effect on historical rankings has rarely been quantified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Obtain per-case metric outputs or public predictions for one benchmark with absent structures; recompute aggregates under each convention; report ranking permutations.
main_risk: Access to per-case outputs of past submissions may be limited.
community_default_belief: Metric conventions are implementation details that do not affect scientific conclusions.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Absence handling assigns extreme scores (zero or one) to entire cases, so small prevalence differences produce large aggregate swings.
fastest_falsification: If rankings are invariant to convention on all tested benchmarks, the concern is negligible in practice.

one_line: Surface Dice with fixed tolerance is blind to uniform boundary bias: a model can score near-perfectly while being consistently offset inward by a margin-relevant amount.
problem: Tolerance-based surface metrics were designed to absorb annotation noise, but they also absorb systematic bias of the same magnitude, which matters for margins and volumetry.
core_hypothesis: Among models with equal surface Dice at clinical tolerance, signed boundary bias varies widely, and bias, not tolerance-band agreement, predicts volumetric and margin errors downstream.
falsifiable_prediction: Computing signed mean boundary offset for models matched on surface Dice will reveal offsets up to the tolerance magnitude, and these offsets will predict systematic volume errors that surface Dice cannot see.
why_important: Radiotherapy margins and growth measurements depend on signed bias; a metric blind to it certifies unsafe models.
why_possibly_novel: Signed bias decomposition of surface metrics is straightforward but almost never reported alongside them.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate several models on one dataset; report surface Dice, signed mean offset, and volume error; test whether offset predicts volume error among surface-Dice-matched models.
main_risk: Defining signed offset requires consistent inside-outside orientation, tricky for complex topologies.
community_default_belief: Surface Dice at an appropriate tolerance is the most clinically aligned segmentation metric.
why_that_may_be_wrong: It is a symmetric band metric; it treats a systematic 2 mm shrinkage identically to zero-mean 2 mm noise, though their clinical consequences differ completely.
fastest_falsification: If signed offsets among high-surface-Dice models are all near zero, the blindness has no practical consequence.

one_line: Dice-optimized models are biased volume estimators, and for longitudinal change detection a volume-consistency-trained model beats a higher-Dice model.
problem: The clinical use of many segmentations is volumetry over time, yet models are selected by cross-sectional overlap, which does not optimize estimator properties like bias and variance of volume.
core_hypothesis: Overlap-optimal and volume-estimation-optimal models differ; a model trained or calibrated for volume consistency across repeated scans detects true change with higher sensitivity and specificity than the Dice-best model, even at lower Dice.
falsifiable_prediction: On test-retest scan pairs without true change, the Dice-best model will show larger volume test-retest variability than a consistency-trained model, and on longitudinal cases with known change, the latter will classify change more accurately.
why_important: It would decouple segmentation research from a metric that does not represent the dominant clinical task, and define a new optimization target.
why_possibly_novel: Test-retest volumetric reliability is standard in quantitative imaging but is rarely turned into a training objective and compared head-to-head against Dice-selected models.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Use any dataset with same-patient repeat scans; fine-tune one model with a cross-scan volume-consistency penalty; compare change-detection operating characteristics against the Dice-selected baseline.
main_risk: Test-retest data is scarce; consistency training may achieve stability by systematic bias, which must be controlled.
community_default_belief: The best-overlap model is also the best tool for measuring volumes and their change.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Overlap penalizes displacement but not consistent bias or variance structure, which are the quantities that determine change-detection power.
fastest_falsification: If Dice rank and test-retest volume variability rank coincide across models, the decoupling premise fails.

one_line: Typical medical segmentation test sets are statistically underpowered to distinguish methods separated by the deltas the literature reports.
problem: Test sets of 20 to 100 cases are standard, but per-case score variance and inter-case correlation imply wide confidence intervals that papers rarely compute.
core_hypothesis: Under realistic per-case variance, the minimal detectable difference at conventional power on standard-size test sets exceeds a large fraction of published between-method gaps, so many reported orderings are statistically unresolved.
falsifiable_prediction: Bootstrap and permutation analysis of per-case scores from public evaluations will show that a majority of adjacent-rank comparisons on typical benchmarks do not reach significance after multiplicity control.
why_important: It quantifies how much of the literature is decision noise and motivates mandatory uncertainty reporting and larger or sequential test designs.
why_possibly_novel: Power analysis is standard in clinical research but almost absent as a systematic retrospective audit of segmentation benchmarks.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect per-case results from one or two public challenges; run paired permutation tests on all adjacent pairs; report the fraction of resolved comparisons and the minimal detectable difference.
main_risk: Per-case results are not always released; case-level correlations complicate clean inference.
community_default_belief: A one-to-two point Dice improvement on a standard test set is meaningful evidence of a better method.
why_that_may_be_wrong: With heavy-tailed per-case score distributions and small n, such gaps sit inside the sampling noise band.
fastest_falsification: If most adjacent pairs on audited challenges are significant under paired tests, the underpowering claim is exaggerated.

one_line: Topology-correctness should be the primary metric for tubular anatomy because Dice-superior models routinely break vessel and airway continuity that downstream navigation requires.
problem: Vessel, airway, and bowel segmentations feed path-planning and simulation tools that fail on disconnected or merged branches, yet models are compared by overlap.
core_hypothesis: Overlap and topology quality are decoupled across models: within the top Dice cluster, connectivity-error counts vary by large factors, and the Dice-best model is often topology-worse, making Dice-based selection harmful for tubular structures.
falsifiable_prediction: Evaluating multiple public vessel or airway models with connectivity metrics (breakages, false merges, missed branches) will show weak rank correlation with Dice within the top group.
why_important: Downstream procedures fail discretely on topology errors; picking models by the wrong criterion has direct procedural consequences.
why_possibly_novel: Topology metrics exist, but the specific decoupling claim within near-tied Dice clusters, where model selection actually happens, is rarely quantified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On one public airway or vessel dataset, evaluate several checkpoints with both Dice and branch-level connectivity metrics; test within-cluster rank agreement.
main_risk: Topology metrics themselves are sensitive to skeletonization details and need careful implementation.
community_default_belief: Higher overlap implies better usability for downstream tubular-structure applications.
why_that_may_be_wrong: A single-voxel gap barely moves Dice but severs a path; the metrics quantify different physical properties.
fastest_falsification: If topology and Dice rankings agree within top clusters across datasets, Dice-based selection is topologically safe.

one_line: The same Dice value denotes different segmentation quality across resolutions and structure scales, making cross-dataset and cross-modality comparisons systematically misleading.
problem: Dice depends on the ratio of boundary-uncertain voxels to total voxels, which varies with voxel size and structure geometry, yet cross-dataset tables compare raw values.
core_hypothesis: A resolution-and-shape-normalized transformation of Dice (an effective boundary-error thickness) makes cross-dataset model comparisons consistent, and applying it retroactively changes conclusions about which modality or dataset is harder.
falsifiable_prediction: The same physical boundary error will produce predictably different Dice across resampled versions of identical data, and normalized scores will show some tasks labeled hard are geometrically easy and vice versa.
why_important: Resource allocation and difficulty claims across subfields depend on cross-task comparisons that are currently confounded by geometry.
why_possibly_novel: The confound is mathematically obvious but a standardized normalization is not adopted, and its effect on published cross-task conclusions has not been audited.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Resample one dataset at three voxel sizes; apply a fixed physical boundary perturbation; verify Dice divergence; then re-express two published cross-dataset comparisons in boundary-thickness units.
main_risk: No single normalization suits all topologies; thin structures need separate treatment.
community_default_belief: Dice values are comparable across datasets as a task-difficulty and model-quality signal.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The metric conflates physical error with voxel-grid geometry, so cross-grid comparisons measure the grid as much as the model.
fastest_falsification: If fixed physical perturbations yield nearly constant Dice across resolutions for typical organs, the confound is practically small.

one_line: Evaluating on pre-cropped regions of interest inflates reported performance, and whole-scan evaluation including localization reorders methods.
problem: Many pipelines are benchmarked on oracle-cropped inputs, but deployment requires the model to also find the structure in the full scan.
core_hypothesis: Localization failure, not delineation failure, dominates whole-scan error for small structures, so methods optimized and ranked under oracle crops are misranked for deployment.
falsifiable_prediction: For small-structure tasks, the gap between oracle-crop and whole-scan scores will exceed typical between-method gaps, and method ranking will differ between the two settings.
why_important: Benchmarks should predict deployed performance; oracle-crop evaluation structurally cannot.
why_possibly_novel: The crop-vs-whole-scan discrepancy is acknowledged informally but its effect on method rankings is rarely measured systematically.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take methods published with oracle-crop protocols; wrap each with the same simple detector; evaluate whole-scan; compare rank order to cropped ranks.
main_risk: Choice of shared detector influences results; needs several detectors to show robustness.
community_default_belief: Delineation quality measured on crops is the scientifically interesting quantity, and localization is an engineering detail.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Localization and delineation errors interact, and the deployment-limiting factor for small structures is usually finding them at all.
fastest_falsification: If whole-scan and cropped rankings coincide and gaps are small, oracle-crop benchmarking is adequate.

one_line: Unreported test-time preprocessing choices (interpolation order, resampling target, clipping) change scores by amounts comparable to claimed method improvements.
problem: Papers describe architectures in detail but often leave inference-time preprocessing underspecified, though it directly transforms the input and output masks.
core_hypothesis: Across common preprocessing variants, per-method score spread is comparable to between-method gaps, and part of the irreproducibility of medical segmentation results is preprocessing variance rather than modeling variance.
falsifiable_prediction: A grid over interpolation order, resampling strategy, and intensity clipping applied to fixed public checkpoints will produce score ranges overlapping adjacent methods on the same benchmark.
why_important: It reframes reproducibility failures and argues for mandatory preprocessing-sensitivity reporting analogous to error bars.
why_possibly_novel: Sensitivity analyses target hyperparameters and seeds; inference-time preprocessing as a variance source is rarely quantified across methods.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take three public checkpoints; evaluate each under a factorial grid of standard preprocessing variants; report per-method spread versus between-method gaps.
main_risk: Some checkpoints embed preprocessing assumptions, making certain variants unfairly wrong for them.
community_default_belief: Preprocessing at inference is a solved, standardized step with negligible effect on comparisons.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Mask geometry and intensity statistics are directly altered by these steps, and there is no actual standard across codebases.
fastest_falsification: If score spread across the grid is an order of magnitude below method gaps, preprocessing variance is negligible.

one_line: Medical segmentation models are texture-first, position-second, shape-last, inverting the anatomy-prior story used to motivate architecture design.
problem: Architectural work assumes models need and use shape priors, but the actual feature hierarchy driving organ segmentation decisions is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: Controlled cue-conflict volumes (texture of organ A in the silhouette of organ B, at position of A or B) will show segmentation follows texture and position and largely ignores global shape.
falsifiable_prediction: In cue-conflict tests, voxel assignments will track texture and location cues in the majority of conflicts, and shape-consistent assignments will be rare across architectures, including those marketed as shape-aware.
why_important: If shape is barely used, shape-prior architecture research is optimizing an input the network ignores, and robustness interventions should target texture reliance instead.
why_possibly_novel: Cue-conflict methodology is established for natural-image classification but has no standard volumetric segmentation analogue with three disentangled cues.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a synthetic cue-conflict benchmark by organ transplantation in real volumes with texture swapping and displacement; measure cue-following rates for several trained models.
main_risk: Synthetic transplantation artifacts may themselves become cues, requiring careful blending controls.
community_default_belief: Segmentation networks learn and use anatomical shape priors, and better shape modeling is a main path to robustness.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Local texture plus location may be sufficient to minimize training loss, so gradient descent never needs global shape.
fastest_falsification: If shape-consistent assignment dominates in cue conflicts, models do use shape and the inversion claim dies.

one_line: Organ segmentation relies on absolute position in the volume so strongly that synthetic organ displacement breaks segmentation more than removing the organ's internal contrast.
problem: The relative contribution of positional priors versus appearance evidence in volumetric models is unknown, though it determines behavior on anatomical variants.
core_hypothesis: Trained multi-organ models weight location priors over appearance: a normal-appearing organ at an unusual position is missed, while a contrast-flattened organ at the expected position is still segmented.
falsifiable_prediction: Displacement interventions will reduce Dice more than intensity-flattening interventions of matched severity, and the effect will strengthen with more training data as position priors sharpen.
why_important: Patients with anatomical variants, prior surgery, or organ displacement are precisely the difficult clinical cases; positional shortcuts fail them silently.
why_possibly_novel: Positional reliance is suspected but the displacement-versus-appearance tradeoff curve has not been measured as a quantitative property of standard pipelines.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Using deformable synthesis on real CT, create matched intervention sets (displacement grades versus contrast-flattening grades); evaluate several checkpoints and plot degradation curves.
main_risk: Realistic displacement synthesis is hard; blending artifacts must be controlled with sham interventions.
community_default_belief: Models primarily segment what they see, using appearance evidence with priors as mild regularization.
why_that_may_be_wrong: In curated datasets position is almost deterministic, so it is the cheapest feature for the optimizer to exploit.
fastest_falsification: If contrast-flattening hurts far more than displacement at matched severity, appearance dominates and the claim is falsified.

one_line: Segmentation networks do not exploit left-right anatomical symmetry, forgoing a constraint human readers use constantly.
problem: Paired organs offer a within-scan reference (the contralateral side), but whether models use cross-hemisphere information is untested.
core_hypothesis: Occluding or corrupting the contralateral side changes paired-organ segmentation negligibly, demonstrating that models process each side independently and ignore symmetry evidence that helps disambiguate pathology from anatomy.
falsifiable_prediction: Contralateral occlusion tests will show near-zero degradation for standard models; adding explicit symmetry features will improve specifically the pathological-asymmetry cases where one side is abnormal.
why_important: Symmetry is among the strongest free priors in human anatomy; quantifying its non-use identifies concrete headroom rather than speculative architecture changes.
why_possibly_novel: Symmetry has been used in specific lesion-detection systems, but a systematic occlusion-based audit of whether generic segmentation models use it is missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For kidneys, lungs, or hippocampi, evaluate public models with contralateral-half masking and mirrored-input consistency tests; compare against a symmetry-feature-augmented variant on asymmetric-pathology cases.
main_risk: For easy healthy cases symmetry adds nothing, so effects may appear only in scarce pathological subsets.
community_default_belief: Large receptive fields mean networks already integrate whatever cross-hemisphere context is useful.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Receptive field capacity does not imply learned use; loss minimization on mostly healthy data never requires consulting the other side.
fastest_falsification: If contralateral occlusion degrades performance substantially, models already use symmetry and the headroom claim vanishes.

one_line: Organ boundaries are inferred more from neighboring structures than from the organ's own edge contrast, so context corruption transfers errors across organs.
problem: It is unknown whether models delineate an organ from its own boundary evidence or triangulate from adjacent structures, which determines how errors propagate.
core_hypothesis: For low-contrast organs, occluding adjacent anchor structures degrades target segmentation more than degrading the target's own boundary contrast, and errors in one organ's segmentation predict correlated errors in its neighbors.
falsifiable_prediction: Neighbor-occlusion will beat self-degradation in induced error for organs like pancreas or esophagus, and cross-organ error correlations in standard test sets will match the anatomical adjacency graph.
why_important: It reframes multi-organ segmentation as a structured inference problem where failures cascade, informing both evaluation (correlated failures) and safety analysis.
why_possibly_novel: Context reliance is generically acknowledged, but organ-level dependency graphs estimated by intervention are not part of current analysis practice.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On abdominal CT, run paired interventions (neighbor occlusion versus matched self-contrast reduction) for three low-contrast organs across public checkpoints; estimate the dependency graph from induced errors.
main_risk: Occlusion severity matching between interventions is nontrivial and drives the comparison.
community_default_belief: Each organ is segmented mainly from its own boundary evidence, with context as secondary support.
why_that_may_be_wrong: For organs whose boundaries are nearly invisible, adjacent high-contrast structures are the only reliable evidence, and models learn to use them as landmarks.
fastest_falsification: If self-degradation dominates neighbor occlusion for all tested organs, the triangulation claim fails.

one_line: Scanner-conditional performance differences persist after intensity harmonization because models key on reconstruction-kernel texture, not intensity distributions.
problem: Harmonization research targets intensity histograms, but CT reconstruction kernels and MR sequences imprint spatial-frequency texture that histogram methods cannot touch.
core_hypothesis: The dominant learnable scanner fingerprint lives in local noise texture and edge response; models exploit it, and harmonizing intensities while leaving texture intact leaves the cross-scanner gap largely unchanged.
falsifiable_prediction: On paired reconstructions of identical raw data with different kernels, segmentation outputs will differ systematically after histogram harmonization, and texture-targeted normalization will close more of the gap than intensity harmonization.
why_important: It redirects the harmonization literature from histograms to noise-texture physics, with direct impact on multi-site deployment.
why_possibly_novel: Kernel-paired reconstructions provide a clean causal isolation of texture that harmonization studies, which usually compare different patients across sites, cannot achieve.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect or reconstruct kernel-paired CT volumes of the same acquisitions; evaluate fixed models on both after intensity harmonization; quantify residual output divergence attributable to texture.
main_risk: Access to raw projection data or paired reconstructions is limited to collaborating sites.
community_default_belief: Intensity normalization and histogram matching address the main scanner-shift component for segmentation.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Convolutional features are spatial-frequency analyzers, so kernel-induced texture is a first-class feature to them even at identical intensity histograms.
fastest_falsification: If outputs on kernel-paired volumes are nearly identical after intensity harmonization, texture reliance is negligible.

one_line: Organ models trained on mostly healthy anatomy actively inpaint lesions away rather than failing randomly, following a learned healthy-anatomy prior.
problem: How organ segmentation behaves on pathological tissue is usually reported as a performance drop, without characterizing the direction and structure of the failure.
core_hypothesis: The failure is generative in character: models complete the organ as if healthy, smoothly interpolating over lesions and reproducing plausible-but-wrong boundaries, which is more dangerous than noisy failure because it looks credible.
falsifiable_prediction: With synthetic lesion insertion of graded size, model outputs will track the pre-insertion healthy contour rather than the true post-insertion boundary, with a sharp transition at a lesion-size threshold, and output plausibility ratings by blinded readers will stay high while accuracy collapses.
why_important: Plausible hallucination defeats human review; quantifying the healthy-prior bias defines a concrete safety test for regulatory evaluation.
why_possibly_novel: Hallucination is studied in reconstruction and generation, but healthy-completion as the characteristic failure mode of discriminative organ segmentation is not an established, measured phenomenon.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Insert graded synthetic lesions at organ boundaries in held-out CT or MR; measure whether model contours follow healthy or actual boundaries; run a small blinded plausibility read.
main_risk: Synthetic lesions may be detectably artificial; needs validation on a small real pathological subset.
community_default_belief: On pathological cases models simply get worse, producing lower-quality but essentially noisy outputs.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Training on predominantly healthy anatomy teaches a strong shape-completion prior that dominates when local evidence becomes ambiguous.
fastest_falsification: If outputs on lesion-inserted cases are noisy rather than healthy-shaped, the inpainting characterization fails.

one_line: For most organs, 3D context only matters within a thin band near through-plane boundaries, so full-3D models spend their compute on a few percent of voxels.
problem: The 2D-versus-3D debate is argued via aggregate benchmark scores, without localizing where 3D context actually changes decisions.
core_hypothesis: Voxelwise disagreement between matched 2D and 3D models concentrates in a narrow band at surfaces nearly parallel to the slicing plane, implying a hybrid that applies 3D reasoning only in that band matches full-3D accuracy at a fraction of the cost.
falsifiable_prediction: Disagreement maps between 2D and 3D variants will show strong concentration near through-plane boundary bands, and a band-limited 3D correction of 2D outputs will recover most of the 3D advantage.
why_important: It converts an ideological architecture debate into a measurable spatial question and offers large inference savings for deployment.
why_possibly_novel: 2D-3D comparisons abound, but spatial localization of their disagreement and band-limited hybrids as a test of the localization claim are uncommon.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched 2D and 3D models on one multi-organ dataset; compute where predictions differ; implement a band-restricted 3D refinement and measure recovered accuracy versus compute.
main_risk: For inherently 3D structures like vessels the band assumption fails, bounding the claim's scope.
community_default_belief: 3D context is broadly useful throughout the volume, justifying fully 3D architectures.
why_that_may_be_wrong: In-plane evidence suffices almost everywhere; only geometrically degenerate viewing directions need cross-slice integration.
fastest_falsification: If 2D-3D disagreement is spatially diffuse rather than band-concentrated, the localization premise is wrong.

one_line: 3D transformer segmentation models have effective receptive fields that collapse to local neighborhoods, contradicting the long-range-context motivation for their use.
problem: Volumetric transformers are justified by global attention, but whether trained models actually consult distant voxels for decisions is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: After training on standard medical datasets, attention-based volumetric models make decisions from effectively local evidence: perturbing or masking voxels beyond a small radius changes almost no predictions, matching CNN behavior.
falsifiable_prediction: Systematic distant-context masking will alter under a small fraction of voxel decisions for trained volumetric transformers, and their measured effective receptive fields will be similar to same-scale CNNs despite architectural global reach.
why_important: If global attention is unused, the field pays quadratic costs for an unrealized capability, and the honest research question becomes why medical data does not induce long-range feature use.
why_possibly_novel: Effective-receptive-field analysis is standard for CNNs; applying causal masking analysis to trained 3D medical transformers with matched-CNN controls is rarely done.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take public transformer and CNN segmentation checkpoints; measure prediction change under randomized distant-region masking at multiple radii; compare effective context curves.
main_risk: Masking introduces distribution shift; needs replacement with plausible tissue rather than zeros.
community_default_belief: Attention architectures win in medical segmentation because they exploit long-range anatomical context.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Training objectives are satisfiable with local evidence, so long-range attention may converge to redundant or local patterns; benefits may come from optimization or capacity effects instead.
fastest_falsification: If distant masking substantially changes many predictions for transformers but not CNNs, long-range context is real and the collapse claim dies.

one_line: CT models exploit absolute HU values as a shortcut, making them fragile to small calibration shifts that human readers absorb without noticing.
problem: CT is nominally calibrated, so models can safely fit absolute intensity thresholds, but real-world calibration varies with scanner state, patient size, and reconstruction, and model sensitivity to this is uncharacterized.
core_hypothesis: Segmentation decisions for low-contrast soft-tissue boundaries depend on absolute HU with near-threshold behavior; global shifts within plausible calibration tolerance produce disproportionate, spatially structured errors.
falsifiable_prediction: Applying small global HU offsets will degrade low-contrast organ segmentation nonlinearly with sharp transitions, while high-contrast structures remain stable, and models trained with intensity-shift augmentation will show flat response at slight base accuracy cost.
why_important: Calibration drift is ubiquitous and invisible; a threshold-brittle model can silently fail on a miscalibrated scanner while passing all geometric QA.
why_possibly_novel: Intensity augmentation is common, but a quantified brittleness curve tied to realistic calibration physics, per structure, is not standard reporting.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate public abdominal CT models under graded global and size-dependent HU perturbations; report per-organ degradation curves and identify threshold behavior.
main_risk: Realistic calibration-error models are needed; naive global shifts may overstate or understate the effect.
community_default_belief: CT calibration makes absolute intensity a reliable feature, and standard augmentation covers residual variation.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Optimization prefers precise thresholds on calibrated data, producing knife-edge decision surfaces exactly at soft-tissue contrasts where calibration error is comparable to the contrast itself.
fastest_falsification: If degradation under plausible offsets is linear and mild for all organs, the brittleness claim fails.

one_line: Because MR intensities are uncalibrated, MR-trained models are forced into geometry-reliant strategies and transfer shape knowledge across domains better than CT-trained models.
problem: The effect of modality intensity semantics (calibrated CT versus relative MR) on what strategies networks learn has not been isolated as a variable.
core_hypothesis: Absence of absolute intensity meaning in MR acts as an implicit regularizer against intensity shortcuts, so MR-trained encoders encode more geometry and transfer better to intensity-mismatched targets than CT-trained encoders of matched performance.
falsifiable_prediction: In matched cross-domain transfer experiments on shared anatomy, MR-source models will retain more performance under intensity remapping than CT-source models, and probing will show higher shape-feature decodability in MR-trained encoders.
why_important: It identifies a modality-level cause of transferability, suggesting intensity-decalibration as a deliberate training intervention for robust CT models.
why_possibly_novel: Cross-modality transfer is studied as a domain-gap problem; the reverse question, which source modality produces more transferable strategies and why, is rarely posed.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched architectures on MR and CT for shared structures (e.g., liver); evaluate both under synthetic intensity remappings and cross-modality transfer; probe encoders for shape versus intensity feature content.
main_risk: Anatomy visible in both modalities differs in contrast structure, confounding a clean comparison.
community_default_belief: CT is the easier, more standardized modality, so CT-trained models are the more reliable transfer source.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Standardization invites shortcut learning; the messier modality may force the more generalizable solution.
fastest_falsification: If CT-source models transfer as well as MR-source models under intensity remapping, the implicit-regularization story fails.

one_line: Segmentation models produce confident organ masks on anatomically impossible inputs, revealing the absence of any global anatomical sanity check.
problem: Deployment safety assumes models degrade gracefully or signal trouble on invalid inputs, but their behavior on anatomically incoherent volumes is undocumented.
core_hypothesis: On shuffled-organ, duplicated-organ, or physically impossible composite volumes, standard models emit high-confidence, well-formed masks, and no internal signal distinguishes these outputs from valid ones, implying anatomical plausibility is not represented.
falsifiable_prediction: Confidence and output-quality statistics on impossible composites will be indistinguishable from valid inputs for standard models, and simple output-side anatomical-consistency checks will catch what model confidence misses.
why_important: It defines a measurable gap between local pattern matching and anatomical understanding, and motivates output-level guards for clinical systems.
why_possibly_novel: Out-of-distribution detection is studied with modality or noise shifts; structured anatomical impossibility as the shift axis is a distinct, largely untested probe.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct composite volumes violating anatomical constraints from real tissue patches; run public models; compare confidence distributions and test rule-based anatomical validators on the outputs.
main_risk: Composites must control low-level artifacts so that detectability is not trivially low-level.
community_default_belief: Softmax confidence or feature-space distance suffices to flag invalid inputs in practice.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Locally, every patch of an impossible volume is in-distribution; only relational anatomy is violated, and nothing in training incentivizes representing it.
fastest_falsification: If model confidence collapses on impossible composites, an implicit sanity check exists and the claim fails.

one_line: Fractional partial-volume-aware labels would leave Dice unchanged but substantially improve derived volumetry, exposing binary masks as the wrong output space at medical resolutions.
problem: At clinical voxel sizes, boundary voxels are tissue mixtures, but training targets force binary decisions, aliasing sub-voxel information into bias.
core_hypothesis: Training on fractional-membership targets (from high-resolution references or mixture modeling) yields near-identical overlap metrics but significantly more accurate and less biased volume and surface estimates than binary training.
falsifiable_prediction: On data with high-resolution reference (thin-slice or micro-imaging subsets), fractional-trained models will cut volumetric bias substantially relative to binary-trained models while Dice differences stay within noise.
why_important: Quantitative imaging endpoints (volumes, thicknesses) inherit avoidable partial-volume bias from binary supervision; fixing the output space is cheaper than resolution upgrades.
why_possibly_novel: Partial-volume modeling is classical in tissue classification but nearly absent from modern deep segmentation supervision design.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Downsample thin-slice data to clinical resolution with exact fractional labels; train binary versus fractional targets; compare volume error and Dice on held-out subjects.
main_risk: Fractional references require high-resolution ground truth, limiting applicable datasets.
community_default_belief: Binary masks at acquisition resolution are the natural and sufficient output representation for segmentation.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Binarization discards sub-voxel information that matters precisely for the quantitative uses segmentation claims to serve.
fastest_falsification: If fractional supervision fails to reduce volumetric bias on resolution-paired data, the output-space critique loses force.

one_line: Resampling anisotropic volumes to isotropic grids destroys information irrecoverably, and native-grid models with anisotropy-aware operators beat resample-then-segment pipelines.
problem: Standard pipelines resample everything to a common spacing as a nuisance-removal step, treating anisotropy as noise rather than as the data's actual sampling geometry.
core_hypothesis: Interpolation to isotropic grids both hallucinates and averages away boundary evidence; operating natively with spacing-aware convolutions or attention preserves decisions that resampling forecloses, especially at through-plane boundaries.
falsifiable_prediction: On strongly anisotropic data, native-grid models will outperform resampled pipelines specifically on through-plane boundary accuracy, and the gap will grow with anisotropy ratio while vanishing on isotropic data.
why_important: Most clinical data is anisotropic; if the first pipeline step throws away signal, every downstream method inherits the loss.
why_possibly_novel: Spacing-conditioning exists in some frameworks, but a controlled information-loss analysis isolating resampling as the causal factor is rare.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take thin-slice data; synthesize anisotropic versions at several ratios; train matched native-grid versus resample-pipeline models; evaluate against thin-slice ground truth stratified by surface orientation.
main_risk: Native-grid operators complicate implementation and may need per-spacing capacity that confounds comparisons.
community_default_belief: Isotropic resampling is a harmless standardization that simplifies learning.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Resampling is a lossy, hallucinating transform applied before the model sees the data, and its errors are unrecoverable downstream.
fastest_falsification: If native-grid and resampled pipelines tie at high anisotropy against thin-slice truth, resampling loss is negligible.

one_line: Super-resolving thick-slice data before segmentation produces confidently hallucinated boundaries biased toward smooth anatomy, worse for safety than honest low-resolution uncertainty.
problem: Super-resolution preprocessing is increasingly used before segmentation, but its hallucinations are absorbed silently into downstream masks.
core_hypothesis: SR-then-segment pipelines transfer the SR prior into boundary placement: errors become systematically biased toward smooth, typical anatomy with reduced apparent uncertainty, degrading exactly the atypical cases while looking better on typical ones.
falsifiable_prediction: On thin-slice ground truth downsampled and super-resolved, SR-then-segment will beat direct thick-slice segmentation on average but show larger errors and misleadingly low uncertainty on cases with atypical fine-scale anatomy.
why_important: The combination of accuracy gains on easy cases and confident failure on atypical cases is the worst possible profile for clinical use, and standard averages hide it.
why_possibly_novel: SR hallucination is known in reconstruction, but its downstream propagation into segmentation bias and uncertainty distortion is rarely quantified case-stratified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a downsample-SR-segment pipeline on thin-slice data; stratify cases by anatomical typicality (autoencoder likelihood); compare error and uncertainty calibration across strata against direct segmentation.
main_risk: Typicality stratification is itself model-based and needs validation.
community_default_belief: Super-resolution preprocessing is a net win for segmentation on thick-slice data.
why_that_may_be_wrong: SR optimizes plausibility under a learned prior, which is anti-correlated with truth precisely when anatomy is unusual, and downstream models cannot distinguish hallucinated from measured evidence.
fastest_falsification: If SR-then-segment matches or beats direct segmentation uniformly across typicality strata with calibrated uncertainty, the safety concern is unfounded.

one_line: Patch-based training makes global constraints unlearnable in principle, and this, not architecture, is the root cause of topology and count errors in volumetric segmentation.
problem: Memory limits force patch training, but no analysis attributes which error classes are caused by never seeing whole structures during optimization.
core_hypothesis: Errors violating whole-structure properties (connectivity, uniqueness, closed surfaces, volume conservation) are predominantly artifacts of patchwise objectives; brief full-volume fine-tuning at low resolution reduces them disproportionately compared to any patch-level intervention.
falsifiable_prediction: Across architectures, global-constraint violation rates will correlate with patch-size-to-structure-size ratio, and a cheap full-volume low-resolution fine-tuning stage will cut violations substantially without changing voxel accuracy.
why_important: It reattributes a known failure class from architecture choice to training protocol, with a cheap fix and clear implications for how 3D pipelines should be staged.
why_possibly_novel: Patch training is universal and its statistical consequences for global mask properties are almost never isolated experimentally.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train the same model at several patch sizes on one dataset; measure violation-rate versus patch-ratio curves; add low-resolution full-volume fine-tuning and measure differential improvement on global versus local error metrics.
main_risk: Low-resolution fine-tuning may fix topology while introducing resolution artifacts, requiring careful evaluation separation.
community_default_belief: Topology errors call for topology-aware losses or architectures.
why_that_may_be_wrong: No local loss can enforce a property the optimizer never observes; the deficiency is in the data view, not the objective.
fastest_falsification: If violation rates are independent of patch size, the patch-cause hypothesis is wrong.

one_line: Sliding-window inference leaves grid-aligned artifacts, and part of what is reported as model uncertainty is actually window-placement variance.
problem: Overlapping-window blending is the universal 3D inference method, but its systematic spatial artifacts are unquantified and conflated with model properties.
core_hypothesis: Prediction differences under shifted window grids are substantial near window boundaries, correlate with reported uncertainty maps, and grid-shift ensembling both removes artifacts and reveals that some published uncertainty signal is inference-protocol variance.
falsifiable_prediction: Variance maps across shifted-grid inference runs will show window-grid-aligned structure, overlap significantly with MC-dropout or ensemble uncertainty maps, and grid-shift averaging will improve boundary metrics without any retraining.
why_important: Uncertainty maps guide clinical review; if part of that signal is a tiling artifact, both uncertainty research and its clinical use need correction.
why_possibly_novel: Window-blending is treated as solved engineering; its interaction with uncertainty estimation appears essentially unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run any public 3D model with multiple window offsets; compute cross-offset variance maps; measure spatial correlation with standard uncertainty estimates and metric gains from grid averaging.
main_risk: Effects may be small for models trained with heavy overlap and Gaussian blending, bounding the claim.
community_default_belief: Standard overlap and blending make window placement effects negligible.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Boundary effects at patch edges are baked into features, and blending averages logits, not decisions, leaving structured residuals.
fastest_falsification: If cross-offset variance is negligible and uncorrelated with uncertainty maps, the conflation claim fails.

one_line: Models exploit cropping and padding conventions as implicit coordinate encodings, so changing the crop convention at test time silently degrades performance.
problem: Preprocessing pipelines impose consistent spatial framing (body cropping, padding, centering) that gives networks stable absolute coordinates nobody intended to provide.
core_hypothesis: Zero-padding and consistent cropping act as positional side channels; models trained under one framing convention rely on it, and deployment pipelines with different framing induce errors unexplained by image content.
falsifiable_prediction: Evaluating fixed models under alternative but content-identical framings (different margins, offsets, padding values) will change segmentations measurably, with errors largest for organs whose identity depends on position, and framing augmentation in training will eliminate the sensitivity.
why_important: Cross-institution deployment always changes preprocessing code; an invisible coordinate dependency is a reproducibility and safety trap.
why_possibly_novel: Padding-based position leakage is documented for classification CNNs; its magnitude and clinical consequence in volumetric segmentation pipelines is essentially unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take public checkpoints; evaluate under a grid of content-preserving framing changes; quantify output divergence and its per-organ structure.
main_risk: Some framing changes alter resampling too; the experiment must isolate framing from interpolation effects.
community_default_belief: Content-preserving preprocessing variations are harmless to a trained model.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Networks read absolute position from border geometry, and position is highly predictive in curated medical volumes, so the optimizer uses it.
fastest_falsification: If content-identical reframing never changes outputs beyond noise, the coordinate-leakage claim fails.

one_line: Models trained on axially acquired and annotated data underperform on reformatted orientations even after isotropic resampling, because acquisition and annotation biases align with the axial plane.
problem: Orientation is treated as solved by resampling and rotation augmentation, but both the image formation process and annotation practice are anisotropic in the same direction.
core_hypothesis: There exists a residual axial-plane advantage in trained models that persists on isotropic data, caused jointly by slice-direction noise structure and in-plane annotation, and reformat-based label augmentation reduces it.
falsifiable_prediction: On isotropically resampled test data evaluated in axial versus reformatted sagittal or coronal presentations, models will show a consistent axial advantage, and models trained with reformat-consistent supervision will show a reduced gap.
why_important: Many clinical reads and downstream tools operate in non-axial planes; a hidden orientation bias distorts their inputs unevenly.
why_possibly_novel: Rotation augmentation is standard, but the compound acquisition-plus-annotation orientation bias and its persistence after resampling are rarely isolated.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate fixed models on orientation-permuted isotropic volumes with correspondingly permuted labels; quantify the per-orientation performance profile and its response to reformat-augmented training.
main_risk: Orientation permutation on anisotropically acquired data conflates resolution and orientation effects; requires near-isotropic acquisitions.
