community_default_belief: After isotropic resampling and augmentation, model performance is orientation-neutral.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Noise texture, partial-volume structure, and annotation smoothness all carry the acquisition orientation, and resampling does not remove them.
fastest_falsification: If per-orientation scores are flat on near-isotropic data, the orientation-bias claim fails.

one_line: The adult-to-pediatric performance gap in organ segmentation is dominated by scale, not appearance, and pure geometric rescaling recovers most of it.
problem: Pediatric deployment failures are attributed to a broad domain gap, conflating body size, proportions, tissue contrast, and pathology spectrum into one unexplained deficit.
core_hypothesis: The primary failure axis is metric scale mismatch relative to the training distribution; size-normalizing inputs (physical rescaling to adult-equivalent organ scale) recovers the majority of the gap without any pediatric training data.
falsifiable_prediction: On pediatric scans, evaluating adult-trained models after physical rescaling to matched organ size will recover a large fraction of the performance deficit, with the residual gap concentrated in genuinely age-specific anatomy.
why_important: Pediatric imaging is chronically data-poor; if a geometric transform substitutes for data collection, deployable pediatric tools become feasible immediately.
why_possibly_novel: Domain adaptation for pediatrics focuses on appearance and data synthesis; scale as the single dominant factor with a trivial fix is a testable, contrarian decomposition.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble a small pediatric evaluation set with organ labels; compare adult-model performance raw versus size-normalized; decompose the residual by age group and organ.
main_risk: Proportions change with age, not just scale, so uniform rescaling may be insufficient for some organs.
community_default_belief: Pediatric imaging is a distinct domain requiring dedicated data and adapted models.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Convolutional features are scale-sensitive but anatomy-preserving; matching scale may restore the feature statistics models expect.
fastest_falsification: If size normalization recovers little of the gap, scale is not the dominant factor and the decomposition fails.

one_line: Field-of-view truncation is a larger real-world robustness threat than intensity shift, and truncation augmentation beats intensity augmentation for clinical variation.
problem: Robustness research concentrates on intensity and noise perturbations, while everyday clinical variation includes organs cut by scan boundaries, which models handle in unspecified ways.
core_hypothesis: Model behavior on FOV-truncated structures is erratic and bimodal (confident completion or total omission), truncation cases contribute disproportionately to deployment failures, and simple truncation augmentation yields larger real-world robustness gains than standard intensity augmentation.
falsifiable_prediction: On truncation-stratified evaluations, error rates for boundary-truncated organs will be several times higher than matched non-truncated cases, and truncation-augmented training will close more of the real multi-site performance gap than intensity augmentation of matched strength.
why_important: Truncation occurs in a substantial share of routine scans and is fully knowable at inference time, so ignoring it is an unforced error.
why_possibly_novel: Truncation is treated as an exclusion criterion in dataset curation rather than a first-class robustness axis with its own augmentation and evaluation protocol.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Create truncation-graded versions of test volumes; characterize per-organ failure modes; train with truncation augmentation versus intensity augmentation and compare on held-out multi-site data.
main_risk: Curated benchmarks underrepresent truncation, so demonstrating real-world relevance needs clinical-distribution data.
community_default_belief: Intensity and noise robustness are the main practical robustness concerns for deployment.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Geometry violations put models further off-manifold than intensity shifts, and curation hides how common they are in practice.
fastest_falsification: If truncated and non-truncated matched cases show similar error rates for standard models, truncation is already handled.

one_line: Cross-site performance drops track case-mix and disease-prevalence differences more than scanner differences, so much of the reported domain gap is prevalence shift in disguise.
problem: Site-transfer studies attribute performance drops to scanner and protocol shift without controlling for the different patient populations each site contributes.
core_hypothesis: Reweighting or matching target-site cases to the source case-mix (by pathology burden, size, demographics) explains the majority of the cross-site segmentation gap for most organ tasks, leaving a small residual attributable to acquisition.
falsifiable_prediction: Case-mix-matched cross-site evaluation will shrink measured domain gaps substantially relative to naive evaluation, and the shrinkage will exceed what intensity harmonization achieves.
why_important: If population, not physics, drives the gap, domain-adaptation methods are treating the wrong variable and clinical validation study designs need case-mix controls.
why_possibly_novel: Prevalence shift is formalized in classification calibration literature but rarely used as the primary decomposition axis for segmentation domain gaps.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On any multi-site labeled collection, compute cross-site gaps before and after propensity-style case matching on clinical covariates; compare with harmonization-based gap reduction.
main_risk: Clinical covariates for matching are incompletely recorded in public datasets.
community_default_belief: Cross-site degradation primarily reflects scanner and protocol differences requiring image-level adaptation.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Sites differ at least as much in who gets scanned as in how, and harder cases produce lower scores regardless of acquisition.
fastest_falsification: If case-mix matching barely reduces measured gaps on several site pairs, acquisition shift dominates and the claim fails.

one_line: Intensity harmonization can remove the pathological contrast that lesion segmentation depends on, improving cross-site organ metrics while degrading pathology detection.
problem: Harmonization methods are validated on healthy-anatomy consistency, but pathology manifests as intensity deviation, exactly what harmonization is built to suppress.
core_hypothesis: There is a measurable trade-off: harmonization strength correlates positively with cross-site organ segmentation consistency and negatively with lesion segmentation sensitivity, with popular methods already past the harm threshold for subtle lesions.
falsifiable_prediction: Applying standard harmonization pipelines before lesion segmentation will reduce sensitivity for low-contrast lesions relative to raw inputs, while organ segmentation improves, and the harm will scale with harmonization aggressiveness.
why_important: Multi-site studies increasingly harmonize by default; if this suppresses disease signal, scientific conclusions and clinical tools built on harmonized data are compromised.
why_possibly_novel: Harmonization evaluation focuses on removing site effects; systematic measurement of pathology-signal destruction as the cost side is uncommon.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a lesion dataset spanning sites, run matched lesion models on raw versus harmonized inputs at several harmonization strengths; plot sensitivity versus site-consistency trade-off curves.
main_risk: Effect size depends on lesion contrast; conclusions may be lesion-type specific.
community_default_belief: Harmonization is a safe preprocessing step that removes nuisance variation.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Statistically, subtle pathology is indistinguishable from site effects; any operator removing the latter must attenuate the former.
fastest_falsification: If lesion sensitivity is unchanged under aggressive harmonization, the trade-off is negligible.

one_line: Multi-site pooled training plateaus because site-specific labeling protocols conflict, and per-site label heads outperform naive pooling, revealing label shift masquerading as image shift.
problem: Adding more sites to training yields diminishing returns that are attributed to model capacity or image heterogeneity, without testing whether the supervision itself is inconsistent across sites.
core_hypothesis: Sites define systematically different labeling functions for the same anatomy; pooled training forces one network to average incompatible targets, and a shared encoder with per-site decoding heads (or label-convention conditioning) outperforms pooled training on every site simultaneously.
falsifiable_prediction: Per-site-head models will beat pooled models on each site's own test set, and the per-site head offsets will be stable, interpretable contour-convention differences rather than noise.
why_important: It changes multi-site training strategy and implies federated learning underperforms partly for label, not privacy or data, reasons.
why_possibly_novel: Multi-head site adaptation exists for images; framing and measuring it as label-function disagreement with anatomical interpretation of the learned offsets is unusual.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a multi-site labeled dataset, train pooled versus shared-encoder per-site-head models with matched capacity; compare per-site performance and characterize inter-head systematic differences morphologically.
main_risk: Per-site data volume may be too small for stable heads, confounding the comparison.
community_default_belief: Pooling all sites into one training set is the best use of multi-site labels.
why_that_may_be_wrong: If supervision targets conflict, pooling creates an averaging penalty that no amount of data removes.
fastest_falsification: If pooled training matches per-site heads everywhere, label conflict is negligible.

one_line: Contrast-phase variation explains more cross-dataset variance in abdominal CT segmentation than scanner vendor, making phase-conditioning a cheap, ignored fix.
problem: Abdominal CT appearance depends strongly on contrast timing, but phase is rarely modeled, reported, or controlled in segmentation studies, while vendor effects get the attention.
core_hypothesis: Variance decomposition of segmentation error across datasets attributes more to contrast phase than to vendor or protocol, and either phase-conditioning or phase-balanced training removes most of the phase-attributable error.
falsifiable_prediction: On datasets with phase metadata (or phase estimated from aortic enhancement), error stratified by phase will vary more than by vendor, and a phase-input model will beat phase-blind training especially on underrepresented phases.
why_important: Contrast phase is knowable at inference and cheap to condition on; ignoring a dominant variance factor while pursuing expensive adaptation methods is a misallocation.
why_possibly_novel: Phase effects are radiologically obvious but rarely quantified as a formal variance component against vendor and site factors in segmentation.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate phase labels via automatic enhancement measurement on multi-source abdominal CT; run variance-component analysis of a fixed model's errors; train phase-conditioned versus blind models.
main_risk: Phase estimation without metadata introduces noise into the decomposition.
community_default_belief: Scanner and protocol differences are the primary CT domain-shift axes to address.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Physiological contrast dynamics change tissue appearance far more than vendor reconstruction differences at soft-tissue boundaries.
fastest_falsification: If per-phase error variation is smaller than per-vendor variation, phase dominance is refuted.

one_line: Segmentation accuracy is systematically stratified by patient body habitus, and geometric body-size normalization closes gaps that intensity-based domain adaptation cannot.
problem: Fairness auditing in medical segmentation rarely covers body size, though habitus changes organ position, surrounding fat contrast, and coil or dose physics simultaneously.
core_hypothesis: Models encode training-population habitus priors; performance declines monotonically toward both habitus extremes, and a geometric normalization of body cross-section removes more of this than intensity harmonization, showing the effect is spatial-prior driven.
falsifiable_prediction: Stratifying public benchmark performance by automatically measured body cross-section will reveal significant monotone trends, and body-size-normalized inputs will flatten them more than intensity-side interventions.
why_important: Habitus correlates with demographics and disease; a size-stratified accuracy gradient is an equity problem hidden inside average scores.
why_possibly_novel: Bias audits focus on demographic labels; body habitus as a mechanistically explainable, measurable, and correctable stratification axis is largely unexplored for segmentation.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute automated habitus measures on benchmark test sets; regress per-case scores on habitus across public models; test geometric normalization against harmonization for gap closure.
main_risk: Habitus correlates with image quality through dose and coil physics, complicating causal attribution.
community_default_belief: Performance differences across patients mainly reflect image quality and pathology, not body size priors.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Position and context priors learned on mid-range habitus misfit extremes geometrically, independent of image quality.
fastest_falsification: If per-case scores show no habitus trend across models and datasets, the stratification claim fails.

one_line: Deployment performance does not decay smoothly with protocol change but cliffs at specific parameter thresholds, so mapping cliffs is more useful than optimizing average robustness.
problem: Robustness is summarized by average degradation under perturbation suites, presuming smooth decay, while deployment anecdotes suggest sudden failure at particular protocol settings.
core_hypothesis: Model performance as a function of continuous acquisition parameters (dose, kernel sharpness, slice thickness, echo time) exhibits identifiable discontinuity-like transitions, stable across cases, defining a safe operating envelope that average-robustness metrics cannot express.
falsifiable_prediction: Sweeping single acquisition parameters via simulation or reconstruction will reveal sharp performance transitions at reproducible parameter values that differ across models but are stable across patients for one model.
why_important: A verified cliff map converts vague robustness claims into deployable acceptance criteria per scanner protocol, the form clinical physics actually needs.
why_possibly_novel: Robustness work reports aggregate degradation; systematic parameter-sweep phase-diagrams of segmentation models are essentially absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Use simulation or raw-data reconstruction to sweep dose and kernel on fixed cases; plot per-model performance versus parameter; test for statistically sharp transitions versus smooth decay.
main_risk: Simulation realism limits confidence; cliffs may be simulation artifacts without raw-data validation.
community_default_belief: Robustness degrades gradually with distribution shift magnitude.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Feature detectors have thresholds; when a protocol change pushes texture past a detector's operating range, failures switch on collectively.
fastest_falsification: If parameter sweeps show only smooth monotone degradation for all models, the cliff model is wrong.

one_line: Organ models fail disproportionately on patients whose unrelated comorbidities rearrange anatomy, a robustness axis no current benchmark stresses.
problem: Benchmarks curate for the target condition, excluding cases with ascites, organomegaly, hernias, or post-surgical rearrangement that alter the spatial context models rely on.
core_hypothesis: Contextual anatomical rearrangement degrades target-organ segmentation even when the target organ itself is normal, and the degradation exceeds that from matched-intensity perturbations, because learned spatial priors misfire.
falsifiable_prediction: On cases stratified by presence of context-altering comorbidities, target-organ performance will drop significantly even for radiologically normal target organs, and the drop will correlate with a quantitative context-displacement score.
why_important: Multimorbid patients are the norm in real populations; curated-benchmark performance systematically overestimates deployment performance for them.
why_possibly_novel: Robustness benchmarks perturb images synthetically; using naturally occurring comorbidity-driven anatomy rearrangement as the stressor with normal target organs is a distinct design.
minimal_falsification_experiment: From clinical archives, assemble target-organ-normal cases with and without context-altering comorbidities; evaluate public models; regress errors on context-displacement measures.
main_risk: Comorbidity labels require chart review, and target-organ normality must be verified.
community_default_belief: If the target organ is normal, unrelated comorbidities should not affect its segmentation much.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Models depend on neighborhood context and position priors that comorbidities disrupt without touching the target organ.
fastest_falsification: If performance on normal target organs is invariant to context-altering comorbidities, spatial priors are robust and the claim dies.

one_line: Test-time normalization adaptation helps healthy cases but harms pathological ones, because pathology itself shifts feature statistics, creating a safety inversion.
problem: Test-time adaptation via recomputed normalization statistics is a popular zero-cost domain fix, evaluated on average metrics that mix healthy and diseased cases.
core_hypothesis: For pathological inputs, statistic-recomputation TTA partially normalizes away the pathology signal, so average gains decompose into healthy-case improvement and sick-case degradation, inverting the clinical priority.
falsifiable_prediction: Stratified evaluation of normalization-based TTA will show positive deltas on low-pathology-burden cases and negative deltas on high-burden cases, with the crossover tracking the fraction of the field of view occupied by abnormal tissue.
why_important: A method that helps exactly the unimportant cases and hurts the important ones is worse than useless clinically, yet average-metric evaluation certifies it.
why_possibly_novel: TTA evaluations rarely stratify by pathology burden; the mechanistic prediction that adaptation statistics absorb disease signal is specific and testable.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Apply normalization-statistic TTA to fixed models on a dataset with graded pathology burden; report per-stratum deltas and correlate with burden measures.
main_risk: Effect depends on batch composition at test time; single-case versus batch adaptation may differ.
community_default_belief: Recomputing normalization statistics at test time is a safe, generally beneficial adaptation.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The statistics shift TTA corrects is partly caused by disease, so correcting it subtracts diagnostic signal.
fastest_falsification: If per-stratum deltas are uniformly positive across pathology burden, the inversion does not exist.

one_line: Lesion segmentation progress is dominated by detection, not delineation: decomposing Dice shows delineation is near-saturated and methods differ almost entirely in which lesions they find.
problem: Lesion segmentation is evaluated with overlap metrics that entangle finding lesions with outlining them, obscuring what methods actually improve.
core_hypothesis: Across published lesion methods, variance in detection-conditional delineation quality is small, while variance in lesion-level detection is large, meaning the field is unknowingly doing detection research with a segmentation metric.
falsifiable_prediction: Decomposed evaluation (lesion-level recall and precision, plus Dice conditional on detection) across public methods will show detection differences explaining the large majority of aggregate score differences.
why_important: If detection is the real bottleneck, method design, loss choice, and benchmark construction should all be re-targeted at detection sensitivity, not boundary refinement.
why_possibly_novel: Lesion-wise metrics exist, but the decomposition-based claim that delineation is effectively saturated across methods has not been established as a general finding.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Re-evaluate several public lesion-segmentation models on one dataset with matched decomposed metrics; report the variance share of detection versus conditional delineation.
main_risk: Detection-delineation decomposition depends on lesion-matching criteria, which need standardization.
community_default_belief: Better aggregate Dice reflects improved lesion boundary modeling.
why_that_may_be_wrong: A found-versus-missed lesion swings its Dice contribution between zero and high values, dwarfing boundary-quality effects.
fastest_falsification: If conditional delineation varies as much as detection across methods, the saturation claim fails.

one_line: Models are wildly inconsistent at counting lesions across same-patient adjacent timepoints, an instability invisible to Dice but fatal for longitudinal clinical use.
problem: Longitudinal lesion tracking is the clinical use case, yet models are trained and validated cross-sectionally, and their temporal consistency is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: Lesion-count and lesion-identity consistency of independent per-timepoint segmentation is far worse than within-scan noise justifies: small acquisition differences flip detections near threshold, making count changes mostly artifactual.
falsifiable_prediction: On short-interval same-patient scan pairs where true change is negligible, per-model lesion count differences will greatly exceed what test-retest noise predicts, and count instability will be uncorrelated with cross-sectional Dice across models.
why_important: Treatment decisions use new-lesion counts; if counts churn with acquisition noise, cross-sectionally validated models are unsafe for their primary clinical purpose.
why_possibly_novel: Test-retest evaluation exists for volumetry but lesion-identity and count stability as a primary model-selection criterion is largely absent from segmentation practice.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect short-interval or same-day repeat scans with lesions; run public models independently per timepoint; quantify count and identity churn versus a human reader's churn.
main_risk: Truly stable short-interval pathological data is scarce; surrogate perturbed rescans may be needed.
community_default_belief: A model with better cross-sectional lesion Dice will also serve longitudinal assessment better.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Near-threshold detections dominate count changes, and threshold behavior is a different model property than average overlap.
fastest_falsification: If count churn on stable pairs is small and tracks cross-sectional Dice rankings, the instability claim fails.

one_line: The minimum detectable lesion size of a pipeline is set implicitly by loss weighting, not resolution, and can be dialed predictably, meaning current pipelines choose a clinical sensitivity threshold by accident.
problem: Small-lesion sensitivity is treated as a capability limited by data and resolution, though the training objective's size-weighting already determines an effective detection threshold nobody sets on purpose.
core_hypothesis: There is a monotone, quantifiable mapping from loss size-weighting parameters to the lesion-size sensitivity curve, stable across datasets, so the detection threshold is a controllable design parameter with a measurable precision trade-off.
falsifiable_prediction: Training identical models with systematically varied size-reweighting will shift the lesion-size sensitivity curve predictably, and the fitted weighting-to-threshold mapping will transfer between two lesion datasets within measurable error.
why_important: Clinical applications need specified sensitivity floors (e.g., detect all lesions above a size); making the threshold an explicit dial replaces accidental behavior with specifiable engineering.
why_possibly_novel: Size-weighted losses exist, but treating the sensitivity-size curve as a calibratable, transferable function of the objective, rather than an emergent property, is a different framing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On one lesion dataset, train a weight-sweep of matched models; fit the weighting-to-threshold curve; validate the fitted curve's predictions on a second dataset.
main_risk: The mapping may be dataset-dependent through lesion contrast distributions, breaking transfer.
community_default_belief: Small-lesion sensitivity is primarily limited by resolution and data, improvable mainly by architecture or data scale.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Gradient contribution scales with voxel count, so the objective already encodes a size threshold; changing it moves the threshold without new data.
fastest_falsification: If sensitivity curves are insensitive to strong size-reweighting, the objective is not the controlling factor.

one_line: Binary masks are the wrong output space for infiltrative disease: continuous involvement fields match multi-rater behavior and longitudinal biology better than forced hard boundaries.
problem: Diffusely infiltrating pathology has no physical boundary, yet the annotation and prediction ontology forces one, generating irreducible disagreement treated as noise.
core_hypothesis: Rater disagreement on infiltrative margins is structured and graded, consistent with raters thresholding a shared continuous involvement percept at different operating points; predicting the continuous field directly explains multi-rater data with fewer assumptions and yields more stable longitudinal measures.
falsifiable_prediction: A monotone-threshold model over a single learned involvement field will reconstruct individual raters' masks with high fidelity via per-rater thresholds alone, and involvement-field volumetrics will show lower test-retest variability than binary-mask volumetrics.
why_important: For gliomas, fibrosis, and infiltrative tumors, the binary ontology corrupts both training signal and clinical measurement; a validated continuous ontology changes annotation, modeling, and endpoints together.
why_possibly_novel: Soft predictions exist as probabilities of a binary truth; positing and testing that the underlying clinical percept itself is continuous, with raters as thresholders, is a different generative claim.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On multi-rater infiltrative-lesion data, fit the shared-field-plus-thresholds model and test whether it reproduces rater masks better than independent-noise models; compare longitudinal stability of both representations.
main_risk: Validating the field against biology requires histopathology correlation ultimately, which is expensive.
community_default_belief: Segmentation targets are binary regions, and disagreement on diffuse margins is annotation noise to be averaged.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The disagreement has threshold structure, indicating the truth is graded and the binary target is a lossy projection.
fastest_falsification: If per-rater thresholds on a shared field fail to reconstruct rater masks better than noise models, the continuous-percept hypothesis fails.

one_line: Lesion models exploit acquisition-indication cues, effectively learning why the scan was taken, which inflates retrospective benchmarks and collapses on screening populations.
problem: Retrospective lesion datasets consist of scans acquired because disease was suspected; protocol choices, positioning, and coverage encode that suspicion, providing a non-anatomical shortcut.
core_hypothesis: Part of measured lesion-segmentation performance derives from indication-correlated acquisition features rather than lesion appearance, so performance drops sharply on indication-mismatched populations (screening or incidental settings) beyond what image quality explains.
falsifiable_prediction: A classifier will predict lesion-positivity above chance from images with lesions masked out, and lesion-model performance on indication-matched versus screening-population data will differ by more than image-quality metrics predict.
why_important: Deployment targets are often screening or general populations; indication leakage means benchmarks systematically overestimate exactly the deployment setting where tools promise most value.
why_possibly_novel: Shortcut learning is documented for classification (e.g., device markers); indication leakage as a quantified inflator of lesion segmentation benchmarks is largely unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a lesion dataset, mask lesions and train positivity classifiers on remaining context to measure leakage; compare model performance across cohorts with different acquisition indications at matched image quality.
main_risk: Screening-population labeled data is scarce, and masking may leave lesion-adjacent effects as legitimate signal.
community_default_belief: Lesion benchmark performance transfers to any population with similar image quality.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The scan itself testifies to clinical suspicion, and models can read that testimony instead of finding lesions.
fastest_falsification: If lesion-masked positivity prediction is at chance, indication leakage is absent and the inflation claim fails.

one_line: Models learn per-scan lesion-count priors from dataset multiplicity statistics, hurting solitary-lesion cases and inventing company for lonely lesions.
problem: Training sets have characteristic lesion-multiplicity distributions, and whether models internalize count priors that bias per-case behavior is untested.
core_hypothesis: Detection decisions are not conditionally independent given local evidence: finding one lesion changes the model's propensity elsewhere in the scan, matching training multiplicity statistics, which manifests as false positives on solitary-lesion cases and misses on unusually-many-lesion cases.
falsifiable_prediction: Synthetic insertion or removal of one lesion will measurably change model responses to fixed other-site candidates in the same scan, and per-case error profiles will track deviation of true count from the training multiplicity mode.
why_important: Count priors corrupt exactly the clinically pivotal calls (first metastasis, solitary lesion), and the effect is invisible without intervention-based testing.
why_possibly_novel: Contextual conditioning between detections within a scan is discussed in classical CAD literature but essentially untested for modern dense segmentation networks.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a lesion dataset, measure response changes at probe locations under insertion or removal of a distant lesion; correlate per-case errors with count deviation from training statistics.
main_risk: Within-scan conditioning may be mediated by global normalization rather than learned priors, requiring careful controls.
community_default_belief: Voxelwise segmentation treats lesions approximately independently given local evidence.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Global features and normalization couple distant regions, and multiplicity statistics are a learnable regularity that reduces training loss.
fastest_falsification: If distant insertion or removal never changes probe responses, count priors are absent.

one_line: Ensembles disagree exactly where raters disagree: seed-to-seed model disagreement on peritumoral margins is a free, unsupervised map of irreducible ambiguity.
problem: Distinguishing reducible model error from irreducible label ambiguity requires expensive multi-rater data, limiting where ambiguity can be mapped.
core_hypothesis: For ambiguous pathological margins, independently trained model replicas develop anti-correlated boundary commitments whose disagreement pattern spatially reproduces inter-rater disagreement, so seed-ensembles can substitute for rater panels in ambiguity mapping.
falsifiable_prediction: Spatial correlation between seed-ensemble disagreement maps and held-out multi-rater disagreement maps will be high on ambiguous margins and low on clean boundaries, and the correlation will survive across architectures.
why_important: If validated, every dataset gets rater-panel-quality ambiguity maps for the cost of a few training runs, improving evaluation, active labeling, and clinical uncertainty display.
why_possibly_novel: Ensemble uncertainty is standard; the specific claim that seed-level disagreement reproduces the spatial structure of human disagreement, validated against real rater panels, is a distinct and checkable correspondence.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On one multi-rater lesion dataset, train several seeds of one architecture on single-rater labels; compare ensemble disagreement maps against held-out rater disagreement voxelwise.
main_risk: Shared training labels may imprint one rater's style on all seeds, capping the correspondence.
community_default_belief: Ensemble disagreement measures model uncertainty, a different quantity from human label ambiguity.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Where evidence underdetermines the boundary, both humans and models must commit arbitrarily, and the loss landscape's flat directions mirror the percept's ambiguity.
fastest_falsification: If ensemble disagreement fails to predict rater disagreement beyond boundary-proximity baselines, the correspondence claim fails.

one_line: For treatment-response assessment, consistent bias beats inconsistent accuracy: a lower-Dice model with stable errors classifies response better than a higher-Dice model with variable errors.
problem: Response assessment depends on differences between timepoints, so error covariance across scans, never measured by cross-sectional metrics, determines clinical utility.
core_hypothesis: Between-timepoint error correlation varies widely across models and dominates change-detection accuracy, so cross-sectional Dice ranking is a poor and sometimes inverted predictor of response-classification performance.
falsifiable_prediction: On longitudinal cases with adjudicated response labels, model ranking by response-classification accuracy will disagree with Dice ranking, and the disagreement will be explained by measured cross-timepoint error correlation.
why_important: Response assessment is a primary clinical function of lesion measurement; selecting models by the wrong criterion directly harms treatment decisions.
why_possibly_novel: Error covariance across repeated measurements is central in metrology but almost never estimated for segmentation models or used in model selection.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On serial lesion scans, estimate per-model cross-timepoint error correlation via repeat-scan or perturbation analysis; compare response-classification performance against Dice ranking.
main_risk: Adjudicated response ground truth has its own noise, and longitudinal datasets are limited.
community_default_belief: The most accurate cross-sectional model gives the most accurate change assessment.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Change estimates cancel correlated error but are destroyed by independent error; accuracy and error stability are different model properties.
fastest_falsification: If Dice rank predicts response-classification rank across models, error covariance is negligible in practice.

one_line: Clinicians correct AI-drawn contours less than identical errors drawn by humans, so clinical contour distributions drift toward model biases after AI adoption.
problem: AI-assisted contouring assumes human review neutralizes model bias, but automation-bias research suggests review effort depends on the perceived source.
core_hypothesis: For matched error magnitude and type, edit probability and edit extent are lower when errors originate from an AI proposal than from a human colleague's contour, and post-adoption institutional contour statistics measurably shift toward the deployed model's systematic biases.
falsifiable_prediction: In a controlled editing study with source-blinded versus source-disclosed conditions, disclosed AI provenance will reduce corrections for equivalent errors, and longitudinal audit of clinical contours will show convergence toward model-specific bias signatures after deployment.
why_important: Human oversight is the regulatory safety argument for auto-contouring; quantifying its selective failure changes deployment and monitoring requirements.
why_possibly_novel: Automation bias is studied in diagnostic decision tasks, but quantitative contour-editing behavior conditioned on error provenance is largely unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Present clinicians with contours containing planted matched errors, labeled AI or colleague or unlabeled, in randomized order; measure edit rates and magnitudes per condition.
main_risk: Editing studies are labor-intensive and lab behavior may differ from clinical-pressure behavior.
community_default_belief: Human review catches AI errors regardless of their source labeling.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Trust allocation is source-dependent; plausible AI outputs receive reduced scrutiny, exactly as automation-bias literature predicts.
fastest_falsification: If edit behavior is independent of disclosed provenance for matched errors, the drift mechanism lacks its premise.

one_line: Correction time depends on error topology, not error volume, so optimizing models for editability rather than Dice changes which model is best for clinical workflows.
problem: Time-saved claims for auto-contouring assume correction effort scales with error size, but interface mechanics make error structure (scattered islands versus coherent boundary offsets) the real cost driver.
core_hypothesis: An edit-cost model based on error topology (component count, slice dispersion, boundary coherence) predicts correction time far better than Dice or volume error, and model rankings under predicted edit cost differ from Dice rankings.
falsifiable_prediction: Measured correction times across error types will show topology features explaining most variance with Dice contributing little, and at least some model pairs will invert ranking between Dice and edit-cost metrics.
why_important: The economic case for auto-segmentation is time savings; optimizing a metric uncorrelated with time misdirects both research and procurement.
why_possibly_novel: Time studies of contour editing exist descriptively, but a predictive, feature-based edit-cost function used as a model-selection metric is uncommon.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Record editing sessions on outputs of several models; fit and cross-validate an edit-cost regression from error-topology features; compare model rankings under time versus Dice.
main_risk: Edit cost is interface-dependent, so the function may not transfer across contouring software.
community_default_belief: Higher-Dice models save more correction time.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Deleting fifty scattered false islands takes longer than nudging one coherent boundary, at identical Dice impact.
fastest_falsification: If Dice predicts correction time as well as topology features, the editability metric is redundant.

one_line: Interactive segmentation models waste clicks because they model where users click as noise, though click sequences follow predictable clinical attention patterns.
problem: Interactive methods simulate user clicks as random or worst-case error points during training, while real clinicians click according to structured priorities (dangerous margins first, ambiguity second).
core_hypothesis: Real clinical click sequences are predictable from image and task context; training interactive models against realistic click policies rather than random simulation reduces clicks-to-acceptance substantially at fixed model capacity.
falsifiable_prediction: A learned click-policy model will predict actual first and second click locations well above chance, and interactive models trained with realistic simulated policies will need fewer real-user clicks than random-click-trained baselines in matched user tests.
why_important: Click efficiency is the entire value proposition of interactive segmentation in clinical use; misaligned interaction simulation wastes that value.
why_possibly_novel: Click simulation realism is acknowledged as a gap, but treating clinician click behavior as a learnable, structured policy with measurable training benefit is rarely pursued.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect click logs from clinicians editing on one organ task; train a click-location predictor; retrain an interactive model with policy-based simulation; run a small user study measuring clicks-to-acceptance.
main_risk: Click patterns may be user- and interface-specific, limiting policy generalization.
community_default_belief: Random or geometry-based click simulation is adequate for training interactive segmentation.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Interaction efficiency depends on matching the actual usage distribution, and real usage is highly structured rather than random.
fastest_falsification: If clinician clicks are unpredictable beyond error-distance baselines, structured policies offer no headroom.

one_line: AI contouring homogenizes inter-clinician variability, which reduces the statistical sensitivity of clinical endpoints and quality metrics built on natural contour diversity.
problem: Consistency is marketed as an unalloyed benefit of auto-contouring, but some clinical and research processes implicitly rely on independent human variation, such as consensus building and outlier-based quality assurance.
core_hypothesis: Post-AI contour distributions collapse toward the model mode, breaking variance assumptions in consensus algorithms, inter-observer QA statistics, and trial endpoints, in measurable ways that can produce false confidence and missed protocol deviations.
falsifiable_prediction: Institutions adopting one auto-contouring tool will show reduced inter-clinician contour variance with unchanged or increased shared bias, and simulated consensus or QA procedures fed with post-AI distributions will show degraded outlier-detection power.
why_important: Processes downstream of contours assume error independence; correlated errors from a shared model defeat them silently, a system-level risk invisible to per-contour evaluation.
why_possibly_novel: Variance reduction is documented as a benefit; its statistical cost to downstream consensus and QA machinery appears essentially unstudied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Simulate consensus and QA pipelines on multi-observer data versus AI-anchored edited data; quantify outlier-detection and consensus-accuracy changes; validate on any available pre-versus-post-adoption institutional archives.
main_risk: Access to pre- and post-adoption clinical contour archives is institutionally constrained.
community_default_belief: Reducing inter-observer variability with AI assistance is purely beneficial.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Independent errors average out in downstream statistics; a shared systematic error does not, and correlated residuals break the machinery built for independent raters.
fastest_falsification: If post-AI contour variance reduction comes with proportional bias reduction and QA power is preserved in simulation, the concern is unfounded.

one_line: Near-perfect automation degrades human review quality so much that intermediate-accuracy models can yield better final corrected contours than the best models.
problem: Model selection assumes final human-in-the-loop quality is monotone in model accuracy, ignoring vigilance decrement when errors become rare.
core_hypothesis: Reviewer error-detection probability falls as model error rate falls (rare errors get missed), so final-output quality as a function of model accuracy is non-monotone, with a regime where better models produce worse clinically finalized contours.
falsifiable_prediction: In reviewer studies with controlled model error rates, per-error detection probability will decline with rarity, and composite final-quality curves will show a measurable non-monotonic region for realistic review workloads.
why_important: If the effect is real, regulatory and procurement logic of always deploying the most accurate model is wrong, and workflow design (error salience, audit sampling) becomes as important as model quality.
why_possibly_novel: Vigilance effects are known in human factors, but quantified crossover curves for medical segmentation review pipelines are not established.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run a review study where contour sets contain planted errors at varying base rates; estimate detection probability versus rarity; combine with model error distributions to compute final-quality curves.
main_risk: Simulated review sessions may understate real clinical attentional pressures in either direction.
community_default_belief: Deploying the most accurate available model always yields the best final clinical contours after review.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Final quality is model quality times review quality, and review quality is a decreasing function of model quality through attention dynamics.
fastest_falsification: If detection probability is flat across error base rates, the non-monotonicity cannot arise.

one_line: Humans cannot identify which AI contours contain clinically significant errors when the errors are smooth and anatomically plausible, dissociating plausibility from correctness.
problem: Review-based safety assumes visual inspection detects meaningful errors, but modern models produce errors that preserve anatomical plausibility, which is what inspection actually checks.
core_hypothesis: Reader detection of AI contour errors depends on plausibility violations rather than on error magnitude, so smooth systematic errors of clinically significant size evade detection at near-chance rates, while trivial jagged artifacts get flagged.
falsifiable_prediction: In blinded reads of contours with planted errors matched on clinical significance but varying in smoothness, detection rates for smooth-plausible errors will be near chance and far below detection of visually irregular errors of equal or lesser significance.
why_important: It quantifies the ceiling of inspection-based oversight and motivates quantitative independent checks (volumetric trends, cross-model disagreement) as mandatory adjuncts.
why_possibly_novel: Reader studies measure agreement and preference, but the plausibility-correctness dissociation as a measured detection-rate gap for matched-significance errors is a specific untested design.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct contour sets with matched-dose-impact errors varying in smoothness; run blinded expert review; compare detection rates across error styles.
main_risk: Constructing errors matched on clinical significance requires dosimetric or outcome modeling that adds complexity.
community_default_belief: Expert visual review reliably catches clinically important contour errors.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Experts detect implausibility; deep models fail plausibly, so the reviewed property and the failed property no longer coincide.
fastest_falsification: If smooth significant errors are detected as reliably as irregular ones, inspection remains sufficient and the dissociation claim fails.

one_line: Quality-assurance models should predict where clinicians would edit, not where Dice is lost; the two targets diverge and the edit-prediction target generalizes better.
problem: Automatic segmentation QA is framed as reference-free error estimation (predicting Dice or error maps), but the operational question is whether a clinician would change anything.
core_hypothesis: Edit events are a distinct, partially disjoint signal from geometric error, dominated by clinical salience; QA models trained on edit logs identify actionable problems with higher precision and transfer across sites better than error-regression QA models.
falsifiable_prediction: On held-out clinical editing data, edit-trained QA will outperform Dice-regression QA at predicting real edits, and Dice-regression QA will flag many regions clinicians never touch while missing regions they reliably edit.
why_important: QA models gate clinical automation; targeting the wrong objective yields alarms nobody acts on and silence where action is needed.
why_possibly_novel: Reference-free QA literature is metric-centric; using accumulated clinical edit logs as the supervision target is a materially different and newly available signal.
minimal_falsification_experiment: From an institution's editing archive, train both QA variants on identical inputs; evaluate on later months' edits; compare precision-recall for edit prediction and cross-site transfer.
main_risk: Edit logs conflate error correction with stylistic preference, requiring label cleaning.
community_default_belief: Predicting geometric error is the right objective for segmentation QA.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Clinically inconsequential geometric error is noise for QA purposes, and consequential-but-small errors are exactly what geometric regression underweights.
fastest_falsification: If Dice-regression QA predicts edits as well as edit-trained QA, the target distinction is immaterial.

one_line: Merging partially labeled datasets teaches models to suppress specific organs conditioned on dataset fingerprints, a structured bias rather than random noise.
problem: Combining datasets where different structures are annotated forces unlabeled true organs into the background class, and the consequences are treated as mild noise handled by masking tricks.
core_hypothesis: Networks resolve the label conflict by learning dataset-identity features and conditionally suppressing organs that were unlabeled in the inferred source, so suppression follows the fingerprint, not the anatomy, and reactivates when fingerprints are removed.
falsifiable_prediction: Models trained on naively merged partial labels will segment an organ on data resembling sources where it was labeled and suppress the same organ on data resembling sources where it was not, and fingerprint-randomization (style transfer between sources) will restore the suppressed organ.
why_important: Partial-label merging is the standard route to large medical training sets; conditional suppression is a deployment landmine that averaged metrics conceal.
why_possibly_novel: Partial-label learning methods exist, but the specific mechanism claim (fingerprint-conditioned suppression, reversible by style randomization) is a testable causal account rarely articulated.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Merge two datasets with disjoint organ labels; test each organ on both sources and on style-transferred versions; measure suppression and its reversal.
main_risk: Well-designed masked losses may already prevent the effect, making it a critique of naive merging only.
community_default_belief: With masked losses, partial-label merging is a solved bookkeeping problem.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Even masked objectives leave background gradients from co-occurring unlabeled organs in some configurations, and dataset identity is easily learnable.
fastest_falsification: If organ performance is source-independent after naive merging, conditional suppression does not occur.

one_line: Iterated self-training on unlabeled medical volumes collapses shape diversity toward atlas-like average anatomy, quantifiable as shrinking shape-space variance per iteration.
problem: Pseudo-label self-training is the default way to exploit unlabeled clinical archives, but its fixed-point behavior on shape statistics is uncharacterized.
core_hypothesis: Each self-training round smooths predictions toward high-prior shapes, so the predicted shape distribution contracts (variance loss, mode collapse toward typical anatomy), degrading rare-variant performance while average Dice appears stable or improved.
falsifiable_prediction: Tracking shape-descriptor variance of predictions across self-training iterations will show monotone contraction, and performance stratified by anatomical typicality will show growing degradation on rare-variant cases as iterations proceed.
why_important: Archive-scale self-training is how foundation-scale medical segmentation is being built; a systematic rare-anatomy erosion baked into the procedure would be a serious hidden cost.
why_possibly_novel: Confirmation bias in pseudo-labeling is known generically; its specific expression as measurable shape-distribution contraction in anatomy, with rare-variant stratification, is not established.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run three to five self-training rounds on one organ task; compute shape-space variance and typicality-stratified accuracy per round against a fixed labeled test set including variants.
main_risk: Strong augmentation or confidence filtering in modern recipes may mask or prevent contraction, requiring recipe ablations.
community_default_belief: Self-training on unlabeled data is a safe way to improve medical segmentation with scale.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The teacher's priors are recycled as targets, compounding a preference for typical shapes with every iteration.
fastest_falsification: If shape variance and rare-variant accuracy are stable across iterations, the collapse dynamic is not operating.

one_line: Dense 3D labels are mostly redundant: a labeling-budget scaling law shows a few well-chosen slices per volume achieve most of full-annotation performance across organs.
problem: Annotation budgets are spent on dense volumetric labeling by convention, without a quantitative law relating label sparsity to final model performance.
core_hypothesis: Performance as a function of labeled-slice fraction follows a sharply saturating curve whose saturation point is predictable from structure geometry (surface-to-volume ratio and inter-slice correlation), enabling principled budget allocation across structures and cases.
falsifiable_prediction: Controlled sparsity sweeps will show that a small fraction of slices, selected with simple geometric heuristics, reaches within a small margin of dense-label performance for most organs, with the required fraction predicted by the geometric formula across datasets.
why_important: Annotation is the binding constraint in medical segmentation; a validated scaling law converts labeling from craft to allocation problem and frees budgets for case diversity over voxel density.
why_possibly_novel: Sparse annotation methods exist individually, but an explicit, cross-dataset validated scaling law with geometric predictors of saturation appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On two public datasets, train across a grid of labeled-slice fractions and selection schemes; fit saturation curves; test geometric prediction of saturation points on a third dataset.
main_risk: Interaction with model architecture and pretraining may shift curves, complicating a clean law.
community_default_belief: Denser annotation reliably buys better models, so full-volume labeling is the gold standard worth its cost.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Adjacent slices are highly correlated, so the marginal information of dense labels decays quickly, and case diversity dominates voxel density.
fastest_falsification: If performance keeps improving steeply up to dense labeling for typical organs, redundancy is low and the law fails.

one_line: The efficiency ranking of annotation modes (scribbles, boundary tracing, clicks) inverts with structure geometry, so efficient-annotation guidance must be structure-conditional.
problem: Efficient-annotation studies crown single winners (typically scribbles) averaged over tasks, ignoring that time cost and information content of each mode scale differently with structure size and shape.
core_hypothesis: Per-unit-time model improvement from each annotation mode depends on structure geometry: scribbles win for large compact organs, boundary tracing wins for thin or sheet-like structures, and the crossover is predictable, making mode selection a solvable assignment problem.
falsifiable_prediction: Measuring time-normalized learning gains per annotation mode across structures of varying geometry will show ranking inversions at predictable geometric thresholds rather than a uniform winner.
why_important: Annotation protocol design for every new medical dataset currently follows generic advice; conditional guidance could yield the same models at substantially lower labeling cost.
why_possibly_novel: Mode comparisons exist per-task; a geometry-conditional theory of annotation efficiency with tested crossovers is a different level of generality.
minimal_falsification_experiment: With timed annotation sessions on structures spanning geometry classes, train models per mode at matched time budgets; map the winner as a function of geometric descriptors.
main_risk: Timing data is annotator-dependent; needs multiple annotators to separate mode effects from skill effects.
community_default_belief: Sparse scribble-type annotation is the generally most efficient supervision mode.
why_that_may_be_wrong: For thin structures a scribble carries almost no boundary information, while a single traced contour carries nearly all of it; geometry decides the exchange rate.
fastest_falsification: If one mode dominates across all geometry classes at matched time, conditionality is unnecessary.

one_line: A label-free anatomical-consistency battery (containment, adjacency, volume ratios, symmetry) predicts model ranking on unseen sites, enabling annotation-free local model selection.
problem: Hospitals must choose among segmentation models without local labeled data, and there is no validated way to rank models on-site without annotation.
core_hypothesis: Violation rates of hard anatomical invariants computed on unlabeled local scans correlate strongly with labeled accuracy rank, because the same failure processes produce both invariant violations and boundary errors.
falsifiable_prediction: Across multiple sites and public models, the rank correlation between invariant-violation scores on unlabeled data and true labeled-accuracy ranks will be high enough to select the best or near-best model in most cases.
why_important: It converts model procurement and monitoring from an annotation project into a computation, directly enabling safe site-specific deployment choices.
why_possibly_novel: Anatomical plausibility checks exist as post-processing; their validated use as a label-free model-selection instrument with measured rank fidelity is uncommon.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define an invariant battery for abdominal anatomy; on several labeled multi-site datasets, hide labels, rank models by violations, and compare against true ranks.
main_risk: Models could satisfy invariants while being uniformly wrong, decoupling the proxy in adversarial regimes.
community_default_belief: Meaningful model comparison requires labeled local test data.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Anatomy provides hard constraints whose violation is informative supervision that costs nothing to check.
fastest_falsification: If invariant scores fail to predict labeled ranks across site-model combinations, the proxy is invalid.

one_line: Atlas-propagated training labels imprint the registration regularizer into segmentation networks, creating direction-dependent boundary bias that survives training.
problem: Registration-propagated labels are a common cheap supervision source, treated as noisy but unbiased, though registration objectives systematically prefer certain deformations.
core_hypothesis: Smoothness-regularized registration under-deforms into thin protrusions and over-smooths concavities, so propagated labels carry signed geometric bias, and networks trained on them reproduce the registration's characteristic error signature even on structures where direct annotation exists.
falsifiable_prediction: Comparing networks trained on propagated versus directly annotated labels for the same anatomy will show the former's errors concentrating in high-curvature regions with the sign predicted by the regularizer, and error maps will correlate with registration-error maps.
why_important: Large training corpora bootstrapped by registration silently standardize a geometric bias across all models trained on them, a supply-chain problem for label quality.
why_possibly_novel: Registration error is known, but its inheritance as a stable, signed, curvature-localized bias in downstream trained networks is rarely traced end-to-end.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate propagated labels on a directly annotated dataset; train matched models on each label source; compare signed error distributions versus local curvature and against registration residuals.
main_risk: Registration quality varies widely; conclusions depend on the registration stack chosen.
community_default_belief: Registration-propagated labels add roughly unbiased noise that model training averages out.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Regularization is a systematic prior, not noise; it biases every propagated label the same way, and systematic bias is learned, not averaged away.
fastest_falsification: If propagated-label models show no curvature-localized signed bias relative to direct-label models, the imprinting claim fails.

one_line: Measured inter-rater variance predicts each task's data-scaling saturation point, giving an a priori sample-size calculator for segmentation dataset construction.
problem: Dataset builders choose cohort sizes by budget and precedent, with no quantitative tool linking task properties to the data volume at which model improvement stops.
core_hypothesis: Data-scaling curves for segmentation saturate when model-reference disagreement approaches the rater-noise floor, so a small pilot multi-rater study measuring that floor predicts the useful dataset size before large-scale annotation begins.
falsifiable_prediction: Across tasks with different measured rater floors, fitted scaling-curve saturation points will correlate strongly with the floors, and a floor-based predictor calibrated on some tasks will forecast saturation for held-out tasks within useful error.
why_important: Annotation is the dominant cost in the field; predicting required scale from a cheap pilot would prevent both wasteful over-collection and underpowered datasets.
why_possibly_novel: Scaling laws and rater variability are studied separately; welding them into a predictive sample-size methodology for segmentation datasets is largely undone.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For several public datasets with multi-rater subsets, fit data-scaling curves via subset training; test the floor-to-saturation relationship and its predictive transfer.
main_risk: Saturation also depends on model class and pretraining, which may swamp the floor effect.
community_default_belief: More labeled data reliably helps, and required dataset size is discovered empirically after collection.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Once model error is inside the noise floor of the supervision itself, additional identically noisy labels cannot teach anything new.
fastest_falsification: If saturation points show no relation to measured rater floors across tasks, the calculator has no basis.

one_line: Federated segmentation underperforms centralized training mainly because sites label differently, not because optimization is distributed, and protocol harmonization recovers most of the gap.
problem: The federated-versus-centralized gap in medical segmentation is attributed to optimization constraints and data heterogeneity, without isolating label-protocol heterogeneity as a cause.
core_hypothesis: When a subset of cases is re-annotated under one shared protocol, federated training on harmonized labels closes most of the gap to centralized training, showing the bottleneck is inconsistent supervision semantics, not gradient aggregation.
falsifiable_prediction: In controlled comparisons, federated training with protocol-harmonized labels will approach centralized performance, while federated training on original heterogeneous labels will not, with the difference exceeding optimization-side interventions like aggregation-algorithm changes.
why_important: Large collaborative medical projects choose federation for privacy; knowing the real bottleneck redirects investment from federated-optimization research to label-protocol governance.
why_possibly_novel: Federated medical imaging research is optimization-centric; a controlled label-harmonization ablation isolating supervision semantics is rarely performed.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a multi-site labeled corpus, re-annotate a subset under one protocol; compare centralized, federated-original, and federated-harmonized training under identical architectures and budgets.
main_risk: Re-annotation is costly and the harmonized subset may be too small to power the comparison.
community_default_belief: Federated performance gaps stem from distributed optimization and image heterogeneity.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Sites disagree about what the correct mask is; no aggregation algorithm can reconcile semantically conflicting targets.
fastest_falsification: If harmonized-label federation shows no improvement over original-label federation, label semantics is not the bottleneck.

one_line: Voxelwise confidence is spatially miscalibrated in a fixed pattern (overconfident at boundaries, underconfident in interiors), and a distance-to-boundary recalibration outperforms expensive uncertainty methods.
problem: Calibration of segmentation networks is assessed globally, hiding systematic spatial structure in confidence errors that determines whether uncertainty maps are locally trustworthy.
core_hypothesis: Miscalibration is primarily a deterministic function of distance to the predicted boundary, stable across cases and datasets for a given model family, so a one-dimensional recalibration map fixes most of it without ensembles or sampling.
falsifiable_prediction: Calibration curves stratified by boundary distance will show a consistent overconfidence-to-underconfidence gradient, and distance-conditional recalibration will reduce spatial calibration error more than deep ensembles at a fraction of the cost.
why_important: Clinically usable uncertainty needs local validity; a cheap structural fix would make calibrated maps deployable where ensembles are computationally prohibitive.
why_possibly_novel: Global calibration metrics dominate the literature; modeling miscalibration as a stable function of predicted-boundary geometry is a specific structural claim rarely tested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For several models and datasets, compute distance-stratified reliability diagrams; fit distance-conditional recalibration on one dataset and test transfer to others against ensemble baselines.
main_risk: The pattern may be architecture-specific, requiring per-family recalibration rather than a universal fix.
community_default_belief: Improving segmentation calibration requires probabilistic methods like ensembling, sampling, or Bayesian approximations.
why_that_may_be_wrong: If miscalibration is structured by geometry rather than epistemic randomness, a deterministic correction addresses the dominant term directly.
fastest_falsification: If distance-stratified calibration curves vary wildly across cases, no stable structural correction exists.

one_line: Ensemble disagreement in medical segmentation localizes label noise rather than model uncertainty, making ensembles accidental annotation-error detectors.
problem: Ensemble disagreement is interpreted as epistemic model uncertainty, but in noisy-label regimes its actual referent is unclear, which matters for how the maps are used clinically.
core_hypothesis: Voxels of high cross-member disagreement coincide predominantly with reference-label errors and inter-rater ambiguity zones rather than with model-knowledge gaps, so ensemble disagreement is better used for label auditing than for flagging model unreliability.
falsifiable_prediction: On datasets with adjudicated label errors or multi-rater panels, ensemble-disagreement hotspots will overlap label-problem regions far above chance, and using disagreement to prioritize label auditing will find errors much faster than random auditing.
why_important: Misreading the signal leads to wrong clinical workflows (distrusting the model where the reference is wrong); rightly read, it yields a free continuous label-quality monitor for dataset builders.
why_possibly_novel: Ensembles and label noise are both studied, but the identity claim about what disagreement actually localizes in medical segmentation, tested against adjudicated errors, is unusual.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a dataset with known corrected labels, compute overlap statistics between ensemble disagreement and correction sites; run an audit-prioritization simulation comparing disagreement-guided versus random review.
main_risk: Disagreement also concentrates at genuinely hard boundaries, so separating noise-localization from difficulty needs multi-rater controls.
community_default_belief: Ensemble disagreement flags where the model is unsure and likely wrong.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Members fit shared signal but disagree where supervision was inconsistent, so the disagreement map mirrors the supervision's defects more than the model's.
fastest_falsification: If disagreement hotspots show no enrichment at adjudicated label errors, the reinterpretation fails.

one_line: Calibration degrades faster than accuracy under site shift, so confidence-based triage becomes unsafe exactly in the deployment settings it exists for.
problem: Confidence-gated workflows (auto-accept high-confidence segmentations) assume confidence remains meaningful under distribution shift, but the relative degradation rates of accuracy and calibration are unmeasured for segmentation.
core_hypothesis: Under increasing site shift, calibration error grows disproportionately relative to accuracy loss, and specifically in the overconfident direction, so fixed-confidence auto-accept thresholds admit rising error rates that the system cannot see.
falsifiable_prediction: Cross-site evaluations will show calibration-error growth outpacing Dice decline with shift magnitude, with confidence distributions remaining nearly unchanged while error increases, making shifted-site auto-accept error rates substantially exceed source-site rates at fixed thresholds.
why_important: Confidence gating is the main proposed mechanism for scaling automated segmentation safely; if its premise inverts under shift, deployed gates provide false safety exactly off-site.
why_possibly_novel: Accuracy-under-shift is measured routinely; the differential degradation rate of confidence validity versus accuracy for segmentation triage appears rarely quantified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On multi-site data, plot accuracy and calibration metrics versus shift measures for fixed models; simulate auto-accept gates and report realized error rates per site.
main_risk: Results may depend heavily on the calibration method applied at the source site.
community_default_belief: A well-calibrated model's confidence remains a usable safety signal across moderate domain shift.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Calibration is a property of the training distribution; shift breaks the confidence-accuracy link before it breaks the features, and silently.
fastest_falsification: If calibration and accuracy degrade proportionally across sites, threshold-based gating remains sound.

one_line: Abstention mechanisms in medical segmentation preferentially reject pathological cases, converting selective prediction into a care-disparity engine.
problem: Selective-prediction methods are evaluated by coverage-accuracy curves without asking which patients end up in the rejected fraction.
core_hypothesis: Because pathology increases predictive uncertainty, abstention correlates with disease burden, so the auto-processed stream is enriched for healthy anatomy while sick patients are disproportionately deferred, undermining both the clinical value and the equity of automation.
falsifiable_prediction: Across selective-segmentation methods, rejected-case sets will show significantly higher pathology burden than accepted sets, and coverage-accuracy curves recomputed on pathology-stratified subsets will reveal much weaker accuracy gains for diseased cases.
why_important: The clinical value of segmentation is concentrated in diseased patients; a mechanism that systematically defers them makes automation least useful where it is most needed, a fact hidden by aggregate curves.
why_possibly_novel: Selective prediction is evaluated statistically; auditing whom it rejects, framed as a systematic clinical-utility inversion for segmentation, is largely missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Apply standard abstention methods on datasets with pathology annotations; compare pathology-burden distributions of accepted versus rejected cases; report stratified coverage-accuracy curves.
main_risk: For some tasks pathology genuinely requires human review, so some enrichment is appropriate; the question is magnitude and transparency.
community_default_belief: Abstention on uncertain cases is a straightforwardly safe design principle for clinical AI.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Uncertainty is confounded with disease; optimizing coverage-accuracy pushes the sick out of the automated pathway by construction.
fastest_falsification: If rejected fractions show no pathology enrichment across methods and tasks, the disparity mechanism is not operating.

one_line: Voxelwise conformal prediction yields clinically useless margins, but structure-level conformal objects (volume intervals, boundary bands) are usable and transfer across organs.
problem: Conformal methods promise distribution-free guarantees, but the natural voxelwise application in segmentation produces enormous uncertain regions that no clinician can act on, and the right conformal object for segmentation is unsettled.
core_hypothesis: Guarantees should attach to clinical quantities: conformalizing derived scalars and boundary offsets yields tight, actionable sets, and the nonconformity geometry is similar enough across organs that calibration transfers with small correction, unlike voxelwise sets.
falsifiable_prediction: On matched data, voxelwise conformal sets will be an order of magnitude wider than clinically tolerable, while structure-level conformal volume intervals and boundary bands will be tight enough for stated clinical tolerances and hold coverage across organs after light recalibration.
why_important: Regulatory conversations increasingly ask for statistical guarantees; identifying the usable conformal object for segmentation decides whether such guarantees are practical or decorative.
why_possibly_novel: Conformal segmentation work exists but concentrates on pixel sets; a systematic comparison establishing structure-level objects as the practical unit, with cross-organ transfer measurement, is uncommon.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement voxelwise and structure-level conformal wrappers on public models; compare set sizes against clinical tolerance specifications; test cross-organ coverage transfer.
main_risk: Exchangeability assumptions strain under site shift, weakening guarantees exactly where needed.
community_default_belief: Conformal prediction ports to segmentation naturally at the voxel level.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Voxelwise guarantees multiply across correlated voxels into vacuous regions; the clinically decision-relevant quantities are low-dimensional functionals, which conformal handles well.
fastest_falsification: If voxelwise sets are already clinically tight on real tasks, the reframing is unnecessary.

one_line: Displaying voxel-uncertainty overlays misdirects clinician attention toward unimportant ambiguity and away from confident errors, degrading review outcomes.
problem: Uncertainty visualization is assumed to help human review, but its effect on where reviewers spend attention and what they correct has barely been measured.
core_hypothesis: Uncertainty overlays anchor reviewers to highlighted regions, increasing edits of clinically minor ambiguous boundaries while reducing detection of high-confidence systematic errors, so overlay-assisted review can produce worse final contours than unassisted review when model errors are confident.
falsifiable_prediction: In randomized review studies with planted confident errors and benign ambiguity, the overlay condition will show higher miss rates for confident errors and more time on low-impact regions than the no-overlay condition.
why_important: Uncertainty display is being built into clinical tools as an assumed safety feature; if it redistributes attention harmfully under realistic error profiles, the feature needs redesign, not adoption.
why_possibly_novel: Uncertainty methods are evaluated intrinsically (calibration, AUROC); their causal effect on human review behavior and final contour quality is an almost empty experimental space.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run a within-subject review experiment on cases containing both confident planted errors and genuinely ambiguous regions, with and without uncertainty overlays; measure detection rates, edit allocation, and final quality.
main_risk: Effects likely depend on overlay design and training, so results need several visualization variants for generality.
community_default_belief: Showing model uncertainty to reviewers improves the safety of AI-assisted segmentation.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The overlay highlights where the model knows it may be wrong, but the dangerous errors are where it is wrong without knowing, and attention is zero-sum.
fastest_falsification: If confident-error detection is unchanged or improved with overlays, the misdirection concern is unsupported.

one_line: MC-dropout uncertainty in segmentation is predictable from mask geometry alone: a label-free distance-to-boundary null model matches its error-detection power.
problem: Sampling-based uncertainty is computationally costly and assumed to convey model-internal information beyond output geometry, an assumption never tested against geometric null models.
core_hypothesis: For trained segmentation networks, MC-dropout variance is almost fully determined by proximity to the predicted boundary and local contrast, so a two-feature null model reproduces its spatial pattern and downstream utility, implying the sampling adds negligible information.
falsifiable_prediction: A regression from boundary distance and local gradient onto MC-dropout variance will achieve high voxelwise correlation, and error-flagging performance of the null model will be statistically indistinguishable from MC-dropout across datasets.
why_important: If a free geometric surrogate matches an expensive stochastic method, uncertainty research needs stronger baselines and deployments can drop sampling entirely.
