why_possibly_novel: Baselines in uncertainty papers are other uncertainty methods; a deliberately information-free geometric null model as the comparison standard is rarely enforced.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For public checkpoints on two datasets, fit the geometric null on held-out cases; compare voxel correlation and error-detection metrics against MC-dropout.
main_risk: The null may fail specifically on out-of-distribution inputs where sampling might carry real signal, requiring OOD test conditions.
community_default_belief: Stochastic sampling extracts model-internal uncertainty information unavailable from the deterministic output.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Dropout perturbations mostly jitter the decision boundary, so their variance is a geometric echo of the boundary itself.
fastest_falsification: If MC-dropout beats the geometric null clearly on in-distribution error detection, the null-equivalence claim fails.

one_line: Natural-image pretrained segmenters place medical boundaries at the strongest local gradient even when the anatomical definition sits elsewhere, a measurable gradient-seeking bias that fine-tuning attenuates but does not remove.
problem: Anatomical boundaries often differ from photometric edges (outer wall versus lumen, capsule versus parenchyma), and whether pretrained edge priors persist after medical fine-tuning is unknown.
core_hypothesis: Models initialized from natural-image pretraining retain an edge-snapping prior: their residual errors are systematically displaced toward high-gradient interfaces, whereas scratch-trained models show unbiased or differently structured residuals near definition-versus-edge conflicts.
falsifiable_prediction: On structures where the anatomical boundary and the intensity edge are separated (measurable on high-resolution subsets), pretrained-initialized models will show signed error toward the edge significantly more than scratch-trained counterparts at matched overall accuracy.
why_important: Pretrained initialization is nearly universal; a persistent geometric bias inherited from photography would systematically distort structures whose clinical definition is not photometric.
why_possibly_novel: Pretraining effects are studied via aggregate transfer scores; tracing a specific inherited inductive bias to signed boundary displacement on definition-conflict anatomy is a sharper causal question.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select anatomy with documented edge-definition separation; train matched pretrained versus scratch models; compare signed boundary-error distributions relative to the local gradient field.
main_risk: Scratch models may be too weak on small datasets, requiring careful accuracy matching for a fair bias comparison.
community_default_belief: Sufficient fine-tuning on medical data overwrites pretraining-induced biases.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Fine-tuning minimizes average loss, which rarely opposes the edge prior strongly enough at the few conflict voxels to unlearn it.
fastest_falsification: If signed errors near conflicts are identical between pretrained and scratch models, the inherited-bias claim fails.

one_line: Point prompts are ill-posed in medical images because anatomy is hierarchical: prompt ambiguity over nested structures explains most variance in promptable-model medical performance.
problem: Promptable segmentation assumes a click identifies one object, but a medical click simultaneously lies in a lesion, a lobe, an organ, and a compartment, and the model must guess the intended level.
core_hypothesis: The dominant error source for promptable models on medical images is hierarchy-level misidentification, not delineation, so an explicit measure of nested-structure ambiguity at the prompt location predicts per-prompt failure probability across models.
falsifiable_prediction: Decomposing promptable-model errors into level-selection versus boundary components will attribute the majority to level selection, and a hierarchy-ambiguity score computed from anatomical containment will predict per-prompt performance better than image-quality measures.
why_important: It reframes medical promptable segmentation from a domain-gap problem into an interface ill-posedness problem, implying the fix is prompt semantics (level specification), not more medical training data.
why_possibly_novel: Prompt ambiguity is mentioned anecdotally; a quantitative decomposition with a predictive ambiguity score grounded in anatomical hierarchy is a concrete, testable formulation.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On multi-level annotated data (lesion-within-organ), issue standardized point prompts; classify errors into level-versus-boundary; fit and validate the ambiguity-score predictor.
main_risk: Requires datasets with nested annotations at multiple levels, which are relatively scarce.
community_default_belief: Promptable models underperform on medical images mainly because of the natural-to-medical appearance gap.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Even a perfectly medically trained promptable model faces an underdetermined task when the prompt does not specify the hierarchy level.
fastest_falsification: If boundary errors dominate the decomposition and ambiguity scores lack predictive power, the ill-posedness account fails.

one_line: Clicks required by 2D-native interactive models on volumes scale with slice count rather than shape complexity, a click-budget scaling law exposing the 3D economy failure.
problem: Interactive foundation models are adopted for 3D medical annotation without a quantitative model of how interaction cost scales with volumetric structure properties.
core_hypothesis: For slice-wise interactive models, clicks-to-target-accuracy grows near-linearly with the number of occupied slices regardless of per-slice difficulty, whereas natively 3D interactive methods scale with shape complexity, so the crossover defines when 2D interactive tools are economically irrational for volumes.
falsifiable_prediction: Measured click-budget curves will show slice-count-dominated scaling for 2D-native tools (correlation with occupied-slice count, weak dependence on shape descriptors) and complexity-dominated scaling for 3D-propagating tools, with a predictable crossover in cost.
why_important: Institutions are choosing annotation tooling now; a validated scaling law converts tool selection and hybrid design from anecdote to calculation.
why_possibly_novel: Interactive methods report average clicks on 2D benchmarks; a volumetric scaling analysis with structure covariates as the object of study is essentially missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On volumetric structures spanning slice counts and shape complexity, measure clicks-to-accuracy for representative 2D-native and 3D-propagating interactive tools; fit and compare scaling models.
main_risk: Results depend on propagation quality of specific tools, requiring several implementations per class for generality.
community_default_belief: Strong 2D interactive models plus slice-wise application are an adequate solution for 3D medical annotation.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Per-slice interaction cost is bounded below by one action per slice, so volumetric cost is dictated by geometry the 2D model never amortizes.
fastest_falsification: If 2D-native click budgets track shape complexity rather than slice count, the scaling premise is wrong.

one_line: Text-promptable medical segmentation inherits report-language bias: prompted with an organ name, models over-segment the clinically notable part rather than the anatomical extent.
problem: Vision-language training pairs images with clinical text that describes findings, not spatial extents, so the learned grounding of anatomical terms may be systematically non-anatomical.
core_hypothesis: Language-grounded segmentation models bind organ terms to the regions reports discuss (abnormal, enhancing, or symptomatic parts), producing systematic truncation of normal anatomy and inflation of abnormal regions relative to anatomically supervised models.
falsifiable_prediction: Comparing text-prompted masks against anatomical references will show characteristic bias: coverage of abnormal subregions exceeding coverage of normal subregions of the same organ, with the gap correlating to how frequently each subregion is mentioned in typical clinical text.
why_important: Text-promptable interfaces are the proposed universal access layer for medical segmentation; a semantic bias in what words mean spatially would corrupt every downstream use silently.
why_possibly_novel: Report-derived weak supervision is known to be noisy; the specific claim that it shifts the learned referent of anatomical vocabulary from anatomy to notability is a distinct, testable semantic defect.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate public text-promptable models on organs with graded pathology; measure subregion-coverage bias versus mention-frequency statistics from public report corpora.
main_risk: Disentangling language-grounding bias from ordinary performance limits requires careful anatomically supervised controls.
community_default_belief: Text prompts are a convenient neutral interface whose main challenge is vocabulary coverage.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The training signal defines meanings by co-occurrence with clinical discourse, and clinical discourse is about abnormality, not extent.
fastest_falsification: If subregion coverage is uniform regardless of notability, the semantic-bias claim fails.

one_line: Deep features of generalist vision models cluster medical images by modality and texture rather than anatomy, contradicting the assumption that generalist features encode what is depicted.
problem: Medical adaptation strategies assume foundation features contain anatomy-relevant abstractions worth preserving, but the actual organization of those features on medical data is rarely audited before adaptation.
core_hypothesis: Representational similarity analysis on medical images will show late-layer generalist features dominated by acquisition attributes (modality, sequence, kernel) with anatomy decodable only weakly and mainly from mid-level layers, implying adaptation should graft onto mid-level features rather than fine-tune from the top.
falsifiable_prediction: Linear probes will decode modality and scanner attributes from late layers with high accuracy but anatomy identity substantially worse, with anatomy decodability peaking at intermediate depths, consistently across generalist backbones.
why_important: Where anatomy lives in the feature hierarchy dictates efficient adaptation design; the field currently guesses instead of measuring.
why_possibly_novel: Probing studies exist for natural-image attributes; systematic anatomy-versus-acquisition decodability maps across depth for medical inputs are rare and directly actionable.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Extract features from several generalist backbones on multi-modality medical data with anatomy labels; run depth-resolved probing for anatomy versus acquisition attributes; correlate probe profiles with adaptation performance from each depth.
main_risk: Probing decodability is an imperfect proxy for what fine-tuning can exploit.
community_default_belief: Late-layer foundation features are semantically rich and thus the natural substrate for medical fine-tuning.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Semantic richness was optimized for photographic categories; on out-of-domain medical inputs the same layers may default to low-level acquisition statistics.
fastest_falsification: If anatomy decodes strongly from late layers across backbones, the texture-clustering defect is absent.

one_line: Zero-shot foundation-model segmentation quality on medical structures is largely predicted by a simple boundary-contrast statistic, so much of medical adaptation gain is concentrated where contrast is low.
problem: Claims about medical adaptation of foundation models are made per-benchmark, without a quantitative account of which structures were ever hard for zero-shot use and why.
core_hypothesis: A per-structure boundary-contrast measure explains the majority of zero-shot performance variance across anatomical structures, implying foundation models already handle high-contrast medical anatomy and adaptation research should be evaluated specifically on the low-contrast residual.
falsifiable_prediction: Regressing zero-shot per-structure performance on boundary-contrast statistics will yield high explained variance across datasets, and adaptation gains will concentrate in the low-contrast tail, with little gain where contrast is high.
why_important: It provides a null model for adaptation papers: improvements should be reported relative to what contrast alone predicts, deflating apparent progress that merely rediscovers contrast.
why_possibly_novel: Per-structure difficulty analyses exist informally; establishing a contrast-based null predictor as an evaluation standard for medical foundation-model claims is a methodological step not taken.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute boundary-contrast statistics for structures across two public datasets; evaluate zero-shot foundation segmentation per structure; fit and cross-validate the predictor; re-express published-style adaptation gains against it.
main_risk: Contrast interacts with structure size and prompt quality, requiring multivariate care.
community_default_belief: Foundation models need broad medical adaptation because medical images are wholesale out-of-domain.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The models may be contrast-limited, not domain-limited: they already segment anything visible by gradient, and the medical gap is specifically the invisible-boundary subset.
fastest_falsification: If contrast statistics explain little zero-shot variance, the null-model proposal collapses.

one_line: Topology errors are driven by acquisition noise, not model choice: the same model produces different topology on same-patient rescans, so topology losses treat the wrong cause.
problem: Topological correctness research assumes broken connectivity reflects model deficiency, without measuring how much topology varies under input perturbation alone for a fixed model.
core_hypothesis: Topology of thin-structure segmentations is chaotic with respect to input noise: test-retest inputs flip connectivity decisions at weak-evidence points, and this input-driven variance exceeds between-model topology differences, implying stabilization (multi-acquisition fusion, evidence accumulation) beats topology-penalized training.
falsifiable_prediction: On repeat-scan or noise-injected inputs, within-model topology variance (branch presence flips) will exceed between-model differences at matched accuracy, and topology-loss-trained models will show equally high input-driven topology variance.
why_important: If topology instability is input-driven, the field's investment in topology-aware losses cannot deliver reliable connectivity, and the solution space shifts to acquisition and inference protocols.
why_possibly_novel: Topology metrics are evaluated cross-sectionally; the variance decomposition of topology errors into input-driven versus model-driven components appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Using repeat scans or realistic noise simulation on vascular or airway data, quantify topology flip rates within and between models, including topology-loss-trained variants.
main_risk: Realistic same-patient repeat data with thin-structure labels is scarce; simulation fidelity becomes load-bearing.
community_default_belief: Topological errors indicate missing structural priors that better losses or architectures should fix.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Connectivity decisions at sub-resolution gaps are evidence-starved; noise decides them, and no prior can conjure the missing evidence correctly case by case.
fastest_falsification: If within-model topology is stable across rescans while models differ, topology is model-driven and the redirection is unwarranted.

one_line: Below a resolvability threshold, vessel and airway models hallucinate continuity from learned priors, drawing through real gaps and fabricating clinical patency.
problem: Continuity is usually rewarded in tubular segmentation, but real anatomy contains true discontinuities (occlusions, stenoses) whose detection is the clinical point.
core_hypothesis: Models trained with continuity-favoring supervision cannot distinguish resolution-limited apparent gaps from true occlusions, and systematically bridge both, so their outputs are anti-informative exactly for occlusive disease, with the bridging rate a function of an SNR-diameter product.
falsifiable_prediction: On synthetic and surgically confirmed occlusion cases, bridging rates will be high and comparable to bridging of artificial resolution gaps, and will increase after topology- or continuity-regularized training rather than decrease.
why_important: Reporting a bridged occlusion as patent is a direct diagnostic error; quantifying the hallucination regime defines where these tools must not be trusted.
why_possibly_novel: Gap-bridging is discussed as a benefit for noisy data; its characterization as a systematic false-patency mechanism with a measurable operating threshold is a safety-oriented inversion of that framing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Insert graded true gaps into vascular data with known geometry; measure bridging probability versus gap size, SNR, and diameter; validate on a small set of clinically confirmed occlusions.
main_risk: Clinically confirmed occlusion imaging with labels is limited, so synthetic-real correspondence must be established.
community_default_belief: Encouraging connectivity improves tubular segmentation quality.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The clinically critical negatives are discontinuities; optimizing continuity trades exactly those for cosmetic completeness.
fastest_falsification: If models reliably preserve true occlusions while bridging only resolution gaps, they already separate the cases and the concern is minor.

one_line: Shape-prior models trade rare-anatomy accuracy for average-case smoothness, making anatomical variants a predictable casualty of prior-constrained segmentation.
problem: Shape constraints are validated on average benchmarks where typical anatomy dominates, leaving their behavior on congenital variants and post-surgical anatomy uncharacterized.
core_hypothesis: The stronger the shape prior, the larger the performance penalty on statistically rare but real anatomy (horseshoe kidney, situs anomalies, resections), with prior-free models degrading more gracefully, so prior strength is a hidden fairness parameter over anatomical minorities.
falsifiable_prediction: Stratifying evaluation by anatomical typicality will show prior-constrained models beating unconstrained ones on typical cases but losing by larger margins on variant cases, with the crossover shifting monotonically with prior weight.
why_important: Patients with variant anatomy are often those needing imaging most; a systematic accuracy transfer from rare to typical patients is an ethically loaded design choice currently made invisibly.
why_possibly_novel: Shape priors are evaluated for average gains; framing and measuring prior strength as a rare-case fairness dial with explicit trade-off curves is largely absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect variant-anatomy cases for one organ; evaluate matched models across a prior-strength sweep; plot typical-versus-variant accuracy trade-off curves.
main_risk: Variant cases are rare, so statistical power requires multi-institution pooling.
community_default_belief: Anatomical shape priors are broadly beneficial regularization for medical segmentation.
why_that_may_be_wrong: A prior is a bet on typicality; its wins on the majority are funded by losses on the minority, and averages hide the transfer.
fastest_falsification: If prior-constrained models match unconstrained ones on variant anatomy, the trade-off does not exist.

one_line: Mask-to-mesh conversion introduces geometric bias comparable to model error for small structures, so downstream planning error is misattributed to networks.
problem: Surgical planning, printing, and simulation consume meshes derived from voxel masks, but the surface-extraction stage is excluded from segmentation evaluation entirely.
core_hypothesis: Standard iso-surfacing and smoothing pipelines add systematic volume and curvature bias that, for structures below a size threshold, rivals or exceeds the upstream model's boundary error, so end-to-end geometric accuracy is pipeline-limited, not model-limited.
falsifiable_prediction: Propagating high-accuracy masks through standard mesh pipelines will produce geometric deviations comparable to model-error magnitudes for small structures, and end-use error budgets will attribute a large share to extraction parameters rather than segmentation.
why_important: Resources are spent improving models by margins smaller than what the neglected conversion stage destroys; an error-budget analysis would rebalance effort toward the actual bottleneck.
why_possibly_novel: Mesh extraction is treated as solved infrastructure; a quantitative end-to-end error budget from voxel prediction to consumed geometry is rarely performed in the segmentation literature.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take masks with known reference geometry; sweep standard extraction and smoothing parameters; compare induced geometric error against typical model boundary error per structure size.
main_risk: Optimal pipelines vary by application, so the budget must be computed per use case.
community_default_belief: Once the mask is accurate, downstream geometric products are accurate.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Iso-surfacing choices (level, smoothing, decimation) each shift surfaces by voxel-scale amounts, which is exactly the scale of remaining model error.
fastest_falsification: If extraction-induced error is an order of magnitude below model error across sizes, the stage is indeed negligible.

one_line: For scalar clinical endpoints, direct image-to-measurement regression beats segment-then-measure in accuracy and robustness, questioning segmentation's role as a universal intermediate.
problem: Clinical quantities (diameters, volumes, angles) are conventionally derived from segmentations, importing all segmentation failure modes into the measurement, without evidence that the intermediate is beneficial.
core_hypothesis: The segmentation intermediate adds error and fragility for scalar endpoints: direct regression trained on measurement labels achieves lower measurement error and degrades more gracefully under domain shift, because it needs not solve the harder full-delineation problem.
falsifiable_prediction: On matched data, direct regression will match or beat segment-then-measure in-distribution and show smaller degradation under site shift, with the advantage largest for endpoints depending on small boundary regions.
why_important: If confirmed for common endpoints, clinical AI pipelines could skip their most expensive and fragile component, changing both product architecture and annotation demands.
why_possibly_novel: Direct-regression alternatives exist in isolated applications, but a systematic segmentation-versus-direct comparison across endpoint types with shift-robustness analysis is not established practice.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For two endpoints (organ volume, vessel diameter) on multi-site data, train direct-regression and segmentation-derived pipelines with matched budgets; compare accuracy and cross-site degradation.
main_risk: Direct models lack visual auditability, which is a genuine clinical adoption barrier independent of accuracy.
community_default_belief: Segmentation is the natural and necessary intermediate for quantitative imaging measurements.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The intermediate solves a superset of the task; solving more than needed with the same data budget usually costs accuracy on the actual target.
fastest_falsification: If segment-then-measure consistently beats direct regression under matched budgets, the intermediate earns its cost.

one_line: Detecting surgical absence is a distinct capability from segmenting presence: models confidently hallucinate removed organs, and presence-trained models cannot learn absence from ordinary data.
problem: Post-surgical patients (resections, transplants, implants) are common in clinical streams, but training distributions contain few absence cases, and behavior on them is undocumented.
core_hypothesis: Absence is not the low-confidence tail of presence: models produce well-formed organ masks at post-resection sites using contextual priors, and absence recognition requires dedicated negative supervision or explicit reasoning, not more presence data.
falsifiable_prediction: On post-resection cases, standard models will hallucinate the removed organ at high confidence in a large fraction of cases, scaling presence-training data will not reduce the rate, and a small amount of explicit absence supervision will reduce it disproportionately.
why_important: Reporting a removed organ as present is an obvious clinical absurdity that erodes trust and can corrupt automated downstream measurements silently.
why_possibly_novel: Hallucination under absence is anecdotally known, but the claim that absence detection is a structurally separate capability with its own supervision requirement is a testable learning-theoretic assertion.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble post-resection cases for two organs; measure hallucination rates versus presence-training scale; fine-tune with small absence-labeled sets and measure the response.
main_risk: Post-surgical data requires chart-verified surgical history, complicating collection.
community_default_belief: Sufficiently diverse training data teaches models when structures are absent.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Ordinary datasets provide no gradient contrasting presence against surgical absence, and contextual completion actively fills the gap.
fastest_falsification: If hallucination rates fall steadily with presence-data scale alone, absence is learnable implicitly and the separate-capability claim fails.

one_line: Dice loss causes calibration collapse by construction because it optimizes a set statistic, and the community's default compound loss inherits the damage.
problem: The field defaults to Dice-containing losses for accuracy reasons, while separately lamenting poor calibration, without connecting the two as cause and effect.
core_hypothesis: Optimizing set-overlap statistics drives probabilities toward saturation independent of evidence strength, so the standard compound loss produces near-binary confidence; sequenced training (cross-entropy convergence, then brief Dice fine-tuning) preserves accuracy while retaining most calibration, showing the trade-off is schedulable rather than fundamental.
falsifiable_prediction: Across architectures, calibration error will increase sharply once Dice terms activate during training, and the sequenced schedule will retain most of the compound loss's Dice while cutting a large fraction of its calibration error.
why_important: Calibration underpins every uncertainty-based safety mechanism; if the default loss quietly destroys it, a schedule change offers safety gains with no accuracy price.
why_possibly_novel: Both facts are separately noted in scattered literature; the causal framing with a schedule-based decoupling experiment as the test is not standard knowledge or practice.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched models with cross-entropy, Dice, compound, and sequenced schedules on two datasets; track calibration and accuracy through training, especially around Dice activation.
main_risk: Post-hoc recalibration might fix the damage cheaply, making the training-side fix redundant.
community_default_belief: Compound cross-entropy-plus-Dice losses are the best-practice default with acceptable side effects.
why_that_may_be_wrong: One term of the default actively optimizes against calibrated probabilities, an avoidable structural cost most users never measure.
fastest_falsification: If calibration is stable through Dice-term activation, the causal mechanism is not operating.

one_line: Heavy augmentation in medical pipelines works mainly as label-noise regularization, not domain robustness, and boundary-targeted label smoothing recovers most of its benefit.
problem: Aggressive spatial and intensity augmentation is credited with domain generalization in standard pipelines, but its mechanism has not been decomposed against the alternative explanation of mitigating boundary label noise.
core_hypothesis: A large share of augmentation's benefit comes from preventing memorization of noisy boundary labels (by decoupling boundary voxels from exact positions), so replacing heavy augmentation with boundary-band label smoothing recovers most in-domain and part of cross-domain benefit at far lower compute.
falsifiable_prediction: On clean-label synthetic or consensus-label data, heavy augmentation's benefit will shrink markedly relative to noisy-label conditions, and boundary label smoothing without spatial augmentation will close most of the gap to fully augmented training in-domain.
why_important: Augmentation dominates training cost in medical pipelines; understanding its true mechanism enables cheaper training and better-targeted robustness interventions.
why_possibly_novel: Augmentation is evaluated as a monolith; mechanism decomposition via label-noise-controlled experiments is rarely applied to the standard medical recipe.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct matched noisy-label and consensus-label training sets; train with and without heavy augmentation and with smoothing-only alternatives; compare benefit sizes across label-noise conditions.
main_risk: Cross-domain benefits may still require true augmentation, limiting the claim to in-domain effects.
community_default_belief: Heavy augmentation improves medical segmentation primarily by simulating acquisition variability.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Its largest measured effects may derive from regularizing against boundary label noise, a mechanism that cheaper interventions also access.
fastest_falsification: If augmentation benefits are equal on clean and noisy labels, the label-noise mechanism is not the driver.

one_line: Training order over structures matters: learning high-agreement anatomy before ambiguous anatomy transfers a stable boundary policy and improves the ambiguous structures.
problem: Multi-structure training mixes all organs uniformly from the start, implicitly assuming order-independence of what networks learn about boundary placement.
core_hypothesis: Networks trained first on structures with consistent labels develop boundary-decision policies that transfer as useful priors to ambiguous structures, whereas simultaneous training lets ambiguous-label gradients corrupt the shared boundary representation, so agreement-ordered curricula outperform uniform mixing specifically on low-agreement structures.
falsifiable_prediction: Curricula ordered by measured inter-rater agreement will beat uniform mixing on low-agreement structures with equal performance elsewhere, and reversed curricula will underperform both, establishing order-dependence.
why_important: It offers cost-free performance from schedule design and connects curriculum learning to a measurable data property (agreement) rather than heuristic difficulty.
why_possibly_novel: Curriculum work uses loss-based difficulty; using inter-rater agreement as the ordering variable with a boundary-policy-transfer mechanism is a distinct, medically grounded formulation.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a multi-organ dataset with agreement estimates, train uniform, agreement-ordered, and reverse-ordered schedules with matched budgets; compare per-structure outcomes stratified by agreement.
main_risk: Effects may be small relative to seed variance, requiring several replicates for power.
community_default_belief: Structure ordering in multi-organ training is irrelevant; uniform sampling is optimal or at least harmless.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Shared representations are path-dependent under non-convex optimization, and early exposure to inconsistent targets may set poor boundary features that later data cannot fully repair.
fastest_falsification: If all orderings perform identically across replicates, order-independence holds and the curriculum claim fails.

one_line: Minority-structure underperformance in joint multi-organ training is a directional gradient-interference problem, and measuring per-structure gradient geometry predicts which structures suffer.
problem: Small or rare structures underperform in joint training, and the standard remedy is loss reweighting, which assumes the problem is gradient magnitude rather than direction.
core_hypothesis: Per-structure gradients conflict directionally in shared layers: some structure pairs exhibit persistent negative gradient cosine, and it is these conflicts, not magnitude imbalance, that predict minority-structure degradation, so conflict-aware update surgery outperforms any reweighting scheme.
falsifiable_prediction: Measured inter-structure gradient cosines during training will predict which structures lose performance in joint versus solo training better than size or frequency does, and gradient-projection methods will recover minority performance where optimal reweighting cannot.
why_important: Multi-organ models are the deployment norm; a mechanistic account of interference converts an empirical annoyance into a diagnosable, fixable optimization property.
why_possibly_novel: Gradient-conflict analysis comes from multi-task learning; applying it at per-anatomical-structure granularity in segmentation, with prediction of which anatomy suffers, is largely unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument joint training to log per-structure gradient cosines; correlate conflict statistics with joint-versus-solo performance gaps; compare projection-based updates against a reweighting sweep.
main_risk: Per-structure gradient logging is memory-heavy and conflicts may be layer-dependent, complicating analysis.
community_default_belief: Minority-structure deficits in joint training stem from class imbalance and are addressed by loss weighting.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Reweighting rescales conflicting directions without reconciling them; if directions oppose, no scalar weighting fixes the interference.
fastest_falsification: If gradient cosines are uninformative about joint-training deficits, the directional mechanism is wrong.

one_line: Same-patient patches within a batch let normalization statistics encode patient identity, inflating validation scores and understating deployment error.
problem: Batch construction in patch-based 3D training routinely samples multiple patches per volume, interacting with batch normalization in ways never audited for information leakage.
core_hypothesis: When batches mix patches from few patients, normalization statistics become patient-conditional features, models exploit them, and reported validation performance (computed under similar batching) exceeds true per-patient deployment performance, with the gap largest for small-batch 3D pipelines.
falsifiable_prediction: Comparing models trained and evaluated under patient-pure versus patient-mixed batching will show systematic score differences, and inference-time sensitivity to batch composition will reveal that predictions for one patch shift when accompanying patches change patient.
why_important: A silent optimistic bias in the standard training and validation procedure would affect a large fraction of published 3D results and their clinical expectations.
why_possibly_novel: Batch-composition leakage through normalization is documented in other fields (e.g., contrastive learning); its quantification for patch-based medical segmentation appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched models with controlled per-batch patient counts; evaluate under single-patch inference; measure the validation-deployment gap as a function of batch patient purity.
main_risk: Modern pipelines using instance or group normalization may be immune, restricting the finding's scope to batch-norm-based systems.
community_default_belief: Batch composition is a throughput detail with no effect on measured model quality.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Normalization couples all samples in a batch, so batch composition is an input; if it correlates with identity, it becomes a learnable feature.
fastest_falsification: If predictions are invariant to accompanying-patch identity and purity-controlled scores match, no leakage exists.

one_line: Overfitting in medical segmentation is spatially localized to boundary bands while interiors stay underfit, so regularization and early stopping should be spatially targeted, not global.
problem: Generalization is monitored with scalar validation losses, assuming overfitting is a global model state, though the error structure of segmentation is spatially heterogeneous.
core_hypothesis: The train-test generalization gap decomposes spatially: boundary-band voxels show large, growing gaps (memorization of noisy boundaries) while interior voxels remain underfit throughout, implying globally tuned regularization simultaneously over-regularizes interiors and under-regularizes boundaries.
falsifiable_prediction: Voxel-stratified gap curves will show qualitatively different dynamics for boundary versus interior bands across datasets, and spatially weighted regularization (stronger in boundary bands) will beat globally tuned equivalents at matched hyperparameter budgets.
why_important: It replaces a scalar mental model of overfitting with a spatial one, unlocking a family of cheap, targeted interventions and better training diagnostics for the field's standard task.
why_possibly_novel: Generalization-gap analyses are aggregate; a spatial decomposition tied to boundary noise, with targeted-regularization consequences, is a fresh handle on a familiar problem.
minimal_falsification_experiment: During training on two datasets, log per-voxel train and validation errors stratified by boundary distance; then compare spatially weighted versus global regularization sweeps.
main_risk: Boundary bands correlate with class imbalance effects, requiring careful separation of overfitting from imbalance dynamics.
community_default_belief: Overfitting is a global phenomenon adequately monitored by scalar validation loss and controlled by global regularization.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The noise that fuels memorization lives almost exclusively at boundaries, so fitting dynamics must be spatially non-uniform, and a scalar summary averages away the signal.
fastest_falsification: If boundary and interior gap dynamics are parallel across training, the spatial decomposition adds nothing.
